title: The Co-optation of Civil Society: How International Organizations Manage Contention
abstract: How do international organizations manage social discontent while opening their governance processes to civic actors? This essay conceptualizes co-optation as a mode of contention management through which international institutions selectively integrate critical voices into participatory arrangements that channel, moderate, and reframe dissent in more regulated forms of engagement. Moving beyond rationalist accounts that treat co-optation as a strategic exchange between rulers and challengers, the article develops a relational framework attentive to sustained interactions among bureaucratic agents, civic actors, experts, and intermediaries. It argues that co-optation operates through institutional infrastructures and cross-boundary chains that stabilize cooperation, organize access, socialize civic actors, and expose critical claims to filtering and normative alignment. These chains do not eliminate the agency of co-opted actors. Rather, they make agency part of the process through which critique becomes institutionally acceptable. The article contributes to international studies by showing how international organizations manage contention through relational forms of capture, and how advocacy engagement can help stabilize institutional authority.

title: Ontological Security Research in International Politics: Assessing the Evolution of a Research Tradition
abstract: Ontological security has become one of the most dynamic and theoretically rich bodies of scholarship in International Relations (IR), guiding research across levels of analysis and diverse domains of world politics. Given its flexibility, inclusiveness, and epistemological and methodological plurality, however, scholars have raised questions about its coherence and analytical distinctiveness. Existing reviews have thoughtfully mapped its richness and scope, but they have been less able to address a central puzzle: How can ontological security research remain theoretically coherent while becoming increasingly plural? This article addresses this puzzle by drawing on Larry Laudan’s philosophy of science. It explains why Laudan’s framework, rather than the more familiar alternatives—Kuhnian paradigms and Lakatosian research programmes—is better suited to capturing this kind of plural scholarly formation. It argues that ontological security scholarship is best understood as a developing research tradition and theory complex: an open and plural formation that connects different theoretical strands, remains anchored in a relatively stable conceptual core, and evolves through empirical and conceptual problem-solving. Viewed through this lens, the plurality of ontological security research should not be read as fragmentation, but as evidence of a productive research tradition whose development depends on synthesizing theories, integrating concepts, and opening new analytical pathways. The article shows that ontological security scholarship contributes to IR by generating alternative accounts of empirical phenomena, connecting levels of analysis, and bridging epistemological approaches. By tracing this development, the article demonstrates why ontological security research remains coherent despite its diversity and how it equips scholars with conceptual tools to pose and address significant questions in world politics. In doing so, it highlights both the overlooked relevance of Laudan’s framework to IR and the broader disciplinary contribution of ontological security research.

title: Rebuilding Trust in Higher Education: Strategies for Addressing the “Diploma Divide”
abstract: The Trump administration is using all the levers of executive power to intervene in universities, including multimillion-dollar cuts, investigations into federal regulation violations, visa withdrawals for international students, and ideological pressures. The outcome of this fight over the purpose of higher education could shape the sector for decades. This reflection essay argues that these attacks have been facilitated by a decade-long loss of public trust in higher education. It addresses two main questions: Why have colleges and universities lost the support of society, and what should they do to restore public trust? The essay argues that this loss of support is driven primarily by rising costs, perceived ideological bias, and questions about degree value. By situating these discussions within scholarship on polarization, populist backlash, and the “diploma divide,” this essay moves beyond causes to explore sector-specific solutions. These include improving educational access, redefining political messaging, demonstrating nonpartisanship, supporting their communities, redefining diversity to include social class, and bridging the cultural divide to protect the university as a democratic institution.

title: Possessive Familialism and the Crisis of Democracy in the United States
abstract: Amid rising concern over a crisis of democracy in the United States, one point of political alignment across the political spectrum stands out: valorization of the family. This is especially striking because it would seem to conflict with the core ethos of the dominant neoliberal political rationality. We propose that both convergence and crisis are fueled by a logic of possessive familialism. Taking up recent feminist, Marxist, and critical analyses of neoliberalism to situate our claim and tracing the genealogy of this thinking to John Locke, we argue that possessive familialism more aptly describes foundational commitments and assumptions of liberal, and now neoliberal, politics. At the core of the governing rationality of our time, the solo, self-sufficient family obscures the realities of human interdependence and fuels capitalist extraction and accumulation. Feeding the fantasy that individuals, families, and polities survive—and even thrive—absent cross-cutting, overlapping nests of social supports, possessive familialism is the linchpin of neoliberal political rationality that starves democratic imagination, culture, and structures, and fuels the current crisis. We identify five elements of possessive familialism; illustrate its operations through several contemporary examples, including the case for marriage equality and the COVID-19 pandemic; and show how it threatens the very conditions of democratic politics in the US.

title: Salinization and Development,
abstract: Climate change-intensified seawater intrusion creates a dual shock of transitory freshwater shortages and lasting soil degradation. We study its impacts on agricultural production in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta, a major rice exporter. Combining river salinity observations and detailed canal network data to map localized hydrological shocks, we find that salinity reduces rice yields but generates disproportionately larger declines in output and revenue. These losses are driven by a contraction in land under cultivation and limited substitution toward salt-resistant crops, pointing to constrained short-run adaptation. Using household and firm data, we further document reductions in own-farm employment alongside minimal transition to non-agricultural sectors, suggesting frictions in labor adjustment. Beyond income effects predicted by Engel curves, households reallocate expenditures toward healthcare and children’s schooling. The increase in schooling spending is driven by higher participation and may reflect shifts in opportunity costs, though we cannot rule out forward-looking responses.
journal_full: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Matching on Gender and Sexual Orientation,
abstract: We study the mating patterns of non-heterosexual individuals, who represent a significant and increasing portion of the population, particularly among the youth. We estimate a multidimensional matching model of the marriage market where partner’s gender is endogenously chosen conditional on the agent’s sexual orientation, and is subject to trade-offs that depend on both the agents’ preferences and the pool of potential partners. We show that same-sex couples experience lower gains from live-in relationships, a “same-sex penalty”. Absent this penalty, the share of same-sex couples in the U.S. would increase by about 50% (from 1.36% to 2.04% of all couples).
journal_full: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: A Dual Perspective on Community Mobility: Home‐Centric Place Networks and Older Adults' Mental Health in Shanghai During the Pandemic
authors: Felicia F. Tian, Lei Xin, Mengying Zhou, Yuhan You, Chen Yang, Yang Chen
abstract: Older adults' community mobility reflects both spatial and relational aspects of aging in place within urban environments. To capture this duality, we introduce a home‐centric place network framework that links the home to community destinations older adults routinely visit. The spatial dimension is measured using standard movement metrics, while the relational dimension is defined as opportunities for social encounters (sociability) and operationalized as the overlap of neighbors' routine activities across community places. We tested this framework by collecting two waves of GIS‐based mobility data and an online survey from 64 community‐dwelling older adults in Shanghai, a rapidly aging megacity, during the COVID‐19 pandemic. Results showed that older adults' place networks were diverse, but both the frequency of out‐of‐home visits and sociability declined sharply following a major outbreak. Those who were more mobile and sociable before the outbreak experienced greater reductions, and sociability was associated with more negative expectations. As social places became associated with higher infection risk, the pandemic fundamentally altered the relational meaning of community mobility. Overall, our findings demonstrate that a home‐centric place network framework deepens population geography by linking physical mobility, social encounters, and the emotional well‐being of older adults.

title: Afghan as (Racialized) “Other”: Politics of Farsi Academic Knowledge Production on Migration in Iran
abstract: This article critically investigates the politics of academic knowledge production on Afghan migration in Iran, posing the question: how does Iranian academia contribute to bordering strategies that marginalize Afghans? Drawing on a qualitative thematic analysis of 114 Farsi academic articles from the Iranian National Library's database—the point at which thematic saturation was reached within an initial corpus of 210 retrieved by keyword search—this study reveals how scholarly discourses construct Afghans as a racialized and securitized “other.” The analysis identifies five recurring themes: (1) measuring security, (2) measuring difference, (3) the pathology of presence, (4) measuring attitudes, and (5) racism and knowledge production on migration. These thematic findings illustrate how Iranian academic discourse problematizes migration, treating it as a deviation that justifies exclusionary practices. By pathologizing and racializing migration, academic narratives align with state‐driven bordering strategies that dehumanize vulnerable populations and normalize systemic inequalities. The study critiques the ethical failures of such exclusionary knowledge production, emphasizing its role in legitimizing state control and reinforcing public hostility toward marginalized groups. By connecting these findings to global debates on migration and the ethics of knowledge production, this work calls for a reflexive approach to studying migration, one that challenges the systemic injustices perpetuated by exclusionary discourses.

title: Migration and the Geography of Life Expectancy: Selective Sorting and Spatial Dependence Across 172 Countries
abstract: International migration has grown rapidly in recent decades, yet its relationship with population health is difficult to disentangle from the economic, structural and geographic characteristics of the places migrants move to. This study examines whether international migration is associated with population‐level life expectancy after accounting for confounding and the data's spatial structure. Data for 172 countries (189 in the spatial analyses) for 1990–2024 were assembled, combining migrant stock statistics from UN DESA, life expectancy estimates from Gapminder, and economic indicators from the World Bank. The analysis used cross‐sectional and panel data methods (pooled Ordinary Least Squares, country fixed effects, and first differences), spatial lag and spatial error models, spatial panel models, multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR), and an origin–destination analysis of bilateral migrant stocks. Migration and life expectancy were positively associated across countries (r = 0.42, p < 0.001), but the cross‐sectional migration coefficient was reduced by 47% after adjustment for GDP per capita, and no association was detectable within countries over time (fixed effects β = −0.13, p = 0.051; first differences β = −0.04, p = 0.744). Life expectancy was strongly spatially clustered (Moran's I = 0.68), and migration showed no detectable association with life expectancy once spatial dependence was modelled. MGWR indicated that the migration–life expectancy relationship was effectively global in scale and non‐significant, whereas unexplained place effects varied at a sub‐continental scale. Eighty percent of international migrants lived in a country with higher life expectancy than their country of origin. These findings suggest that the cross‐national association reflects the selective sorting of migrants towards already healthier places, compounded by spatial dependence, rather than an independent effect of migration on population health. More broadly, they extend the selective‐sorting framework from the subnational to the international scale and highlight the importance of geographic structure in interpreting migration–health relationships.

title: Moral Narratives, Fragile Rights and Educational Striving Among Floating Lives in Urban Vietnam
authors: Nguyen Hoang Thien, Nguyen Hoang Yen
abstract: This study examines how Vietnamese returnees from Cambodia living on houseboats along a canal in urban Vietnam experience residence and citizenship in everyday life. Water‐based dwelling and cross‐border migration histories combine to produce a grey space in which residents are neither fully recognised nor consistently removed, despite holding Vietnamese nationality. Living on waterways outside planning compliance places households beyond the administrative categories used to distribute welfare, healthcare and residency verification, producing differentiated citizenship in practice. Residents respond through what the study terms moral infrastructure: hardship narratives, accounts of a life that burdens no one, and caregiving responsibilities used as practical grounds for negotiating tolerance with authorities. They also rely on manual work and relationships with ‘quý nhân’ and ‘mạnh thường quân’ (benevolent doctors, donors and volunteers) to meet everyday needs. Education, meanwhile, serves as a future‐oriented strategy through which families hope the next generation will gain the security and recognition they lack. Theoretically, the study extends Yiftachel's grey space framework beyond land‐based contexts and develops Holston's differentiated citizenship by showing that access to welfare depends on residency registration rather than nationality. It also proposes moral infrastructure as a complement to Simone's people‐as‐infrastructure. Practically, it calls for welfare eligibility to be decoupled from residency documentation, governance to be made more consistent and less discretionary and population frameworks to ensure that cross‐border return histories are not treated as a basis for administrative suspicion or unequal treatment.

title: Temporal Access and Gendered Care: Livelihoods, Staying and Migration in Vietnam's Coastal Mangrove Communities
authors: Ly Quoc Dang, Huynh Van Da, K. David Harrison, Mai Phuc Thinh
abstract: Access to coastal resources depends not only on property, governance and proximity but also on whether ecological, household and bodily demands can be coordinated. This article examines how Khmer women negotiate mangrove and marine livelihoods in three coastal phum (villages) in Sóc Trăng, Vietnam's Mekong Delta. Drawing on an ethnographic case study, 13 narrative interviews (7 conducted as mobile interviews), participant observation and informal conversations, it examines temporal access, productive–reproductive coordination and staying or migration. Access depended on aligning tides, weather, routes, transport, bodily capacity, care and market waiting. Childcare, illness, cultivation and ritual obligations shaped whether and when livelihood work could occur. Women's local availability often sustained households while others migrated, although care could also organise collective movement. The article develops chronotopic care to explain this gendered coordination and cautions against equating livelihood continuity with resilience.

title: Reworking Im/Mobility Scripts Across Generations: Leaving, Staying and Returning in Rural Taiwan
abstract: Recent research on rural im/mobility has shown that leaving, staying and returning are meaningful life‐course processes rather than residual outcomes of migration. Building on this discussion, this article develops the concept of rural im/mobility scripts to examine the normative mobility pathways and meanings attached to leaving, staying and returning. These scripts are historically and spatially constituted, but are also reworked through biographical experience as conditions change. Drawing on life‐history interviews with 28 rural returnees and stayers in Yunlin and Chiayi, Taiwan, most born between 1971 and 1990, the analysis identifies 3 interrelated processes across the life course. First, during adolescence, participants inherited a taken‐for‐granted outmigration script in which leaving was highly institutionalised through educational expansion, parental expectations, urban success imaginaries and the devaluation of rural work, yet often weakly planned in practice. Second, in adulthood, they re‐legitimated staying and returning through locally grounded mobility, using transport, commuting, digital platforms, cross‐place markets and skills acquired elsewhere to build adequate lives and pursue local achievement from their hometowns. Third, as parents, they translated their own im/mobility experiences into a conditional expectation of self‐directed mobility for the next generation: children should know their hometown, see the world and ultimately decide whether to leave, stay and return. Following one generation from youth into parenthood, this article shows that rural im/mobility scripts are revised across the life course and translated into expectations for the next generation.

title: Home in Motion: Eritrean Diasporic Experiences and the Negotiation of Home Across Transnational Spaces
abstract: This article examines how unequal legal, economic, and mobility conditions shape homemaking among Eritrea's contemporary ‘generation of asylum.’ Drawing on 160 survey responses and 13 in‐depth interviews, it compares Eritreans living in first‐asylum settings in Uganda and Ethiopia, categorised as OAUE, with those living in European destination settings in Italy and Sweden, categorised as OEUIS. The findings show that political estrangement from the Eritrean state can coexist with enduring affective attachment to Eritrea, while participants’ capacities to establish home in their countries of residence vary substantially. The comparison identifies a ‘proximity paradox’: participants living geographically closer to Eritrea in OAUE may experience weaker host‐country belonging than those living farther away in OEUIS because of greater legal insecurity, restricted mobility, and constrained economic opportunities. These inequalities can also stratify transnational homemaking. Regional cities, weddings and family reunions can provide temporary homing through cultural continuity and familial connection, but access to these spaces is unevenly enabled by travel documentation and economic security. Aspirations for return are similarly conditional on political and legal change rather than expressions of nostalgia alone. The article contributes to migration and diaspora scholarship by conceptualising temporary homing as a provisional and unequally accessible process shaped by migrants’ positions within unequal mobility regimes.

title: Trading migration? Explaining mobility provisions in preferential trade agreements
authors: Philipp Lutz, Sandra Lavenex, Paula Hoffmeyer-Zlotnik
abstract: Notwithstanding a generally unfavorable political climate regarding international migration, preferential trade agreements (PTAs) increasingly include provisions facilitating the temporary movement of specific categories of workers. Today, approximately seven in ten newly concluded PTAs contain clauses that enable the mobility of workers and businesspeople—particularly business visitors and intra-corporate transferees, who constitute a substantial share of skilled temporary migration in advanced industrial economies. This trend is striking given states’ longstanding emphasis on preserving sovereign control over migration policy. This article investigates the drivers of mobility provisions in PTAs and the implications for broader economic and migration policy. We develop and test three theoretical logics: (1) a trade logic grounded in interests resulting from economic interdependence; (2) a politics logic centered on migration control objectives; and (3) an institutional logic emphasizing path dependence and diffusion. Drawing on the MITA dataset, which codes mobility provisions in PTAs globally from 1960 to 2020, we find that economic interdependence and institutional path dependence are the primary forces behind mobility provisions, while migration control prerogatives have little explanatory power for either the presence, scope, or depth of these provisions. Our findings underscore the economic rationale behind mobility provisions in trade agreements, highlighting a pattern of selective liberalization for highly skilled workers and an increasingly fragmented landscape of migration governance.

title: Stefano Recchia. 2025. Strategies for Approval: Building Support for Military Intervention at the UN Security Council. (New Haven: Yale University Press)
Same Race, Different Paths: Socialization, Orientation, and the Black Partisan Gender Gap
abstract: Black women have long anchored Black political cohesion, yet little explains why a gender gap persists within a group marked by strong Democratic loyalty. Drawing on historical and sociological work, we argue that Black women’s collective-first orientation—shaped by gendered social roles across enslavement, Jim Crow, and modern civic life—heightens the political significance of the antecedents of Black Democratic partisanship: racial identity salience, perceived discrimination, and racially homogenous social networks. Using an original national survey of 4,200 Black Americans, we find that the partisan gender gap widens because the composition of their social networks more strongly shapes Black women’s political preferences. Accounting for racial identity salience and perceived discrimination substantially reduces the gender gap. These findings illuminate how racialized gender roles structure the pathways through which group-based norms translate into partisan behavior, providing a mechanism for intragroup variation and guiding more nuanced strategies for political engagement and mobilization.

title: Testifying in Texas: Reflecting on We Testify Texas , a State-based Abortion Storyteller Retreat
abstract: “I want to talk about my complicated feelings and how I was treated during my abortion procedure,” a Texas 20-something declared as they 1 hoisted themself out of the pool’s deep end. Three others considered the proposed topic and quickly tiptoed across the surrounding hot deck toward the shaded chairs to join the conversation. The 22 Texans lounging around the pool deck were part of We Testify ’s first state-based abortion storytelling cohort, We Testify Texas , held at a small retreat center in Mineola, a rural town east of Dallas in 2019. The We Testify Texas program sought to strengthen the state’s robust reproductive justice organizational advocacy infrastructure by training Texans who have had abortions 2 to share their stories and engage with advocacy efforts to preserve and expand abortion access and challenge hostile criminalization efforts in Texas. Although storytelling has been a tactic integral to feminist and social justice organizing (Fernandes 2017; Ganz 2024; Polletta 2022; Ross 2008), nonprofit organizational efforts primarily focused on the production of stories for public consumption, rather than engagement with the storytellers as local experts and organizers. This creates a transactional relationship between advocacy organizations and the people most impacted by the issue, separating storytellers from their stories and leaving storytellers as an untapped resource of testimonial expertise in communities. How can social justice movements and advocacy organizations center people who have had abortion experiences to lead cultural and state-based policy change work? This Notes from the Field reflects on the We Testify storytelling model as implemented through the We Testify Texas program, including the national-local partnership, programmatic activities, impact of the cohort, and how such a program could be replicated in similar political climates and distinct communities.

title: Tragic but Rare: Abortion Storytelling in Local News Coverage One Year Past-Dobbs
abstract: This essay examines local news coverage of abortion stories during the year following the United States Supreme Court decision, Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022), in states with trigger bans and states considering legislation to severely restrict abortion. Framing theory stipulates that news narratives are never neutral. The way stories are structured inevitably foregrounds certain themes while pushing others to the margins (Chong and Druckman 2007; Pope, Pelletier, and Guertin 2018). We analyzed 1600 local news articles 1 for the presence of thematic frames, which focus on the big-picture context of a political event, and episodic frames, which more closely resemble a case study (Feezell, Glazier, and Boydstun 2021; Iyengar 1994). Our initial framing analysis found that only a small handful of articles, 66 out of 1,600, used episodic frames to tell the abortion stories of individuals. 2

title: Why Activist Stories Matter and How They Lead to Change: The Reproductive Privacy Act in Rhode Island
authors: Jordan Banick, Mikaila Mariel Lemonik Arthur
abstract: “ Roe v. Wade is not going to be overturned. I think that’s a concern that’s not founded in reality,” said Rhode Island House Speaker Nicholas Mattiello in 2018 (Donnis 2022). As much as his words stung activists working to protect the right to abortion, they also signaled that he was out of touch with concerns about access to abortion in the nation as well as the state. National polling generally shows that 7 in 10 people support the right to abortion, and the same was true in Rhode Island (Bender 2018). So how did the smallest, most Catholic state in the United States manage to legislatively protect the right to abortion in 2019 without his support or the support of Rhode Island Senate Leadership?

title: Translation in State Governance. By DongshengRen, LinJiao, and SanjunSun, Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 72 pp. US $68.33(hbk). ISBN: 978‐1‐00‐965981‐9; US $23.75 (ebk), ISBN: 2633‐6480
authors: Jiaqi Zhu, Yang Yao, Qiujun Su

title: Climate, Nature, and the Uneven Expansion of Financial Governance
abstract: Financial authorities have developed extensive climate‐related policies, but nature‐related financial policy remains less widespread. Using data on individual policy instruments across 116 jurisdictions from 2000 to 2025, this paper compares the adoption, policy areas, binding status, and source of climate‐ and nature‐related policies. Nature‐related policies appear in 27 jurisdictions, compared with 60 for climate‐only policies. National nature adoption is positively associated with a larger existing body of climate and environmental financial policies, mainly through the broader environmental component rather than climate‐specific policy. Climate‐only policies are used more frequently in prudential supervision and credit allocation than policies that combine nature with climate or broader environmental concerns. Nature‐related policies have a higher mandatory share over the full period but a lower share than climate‐only policies in 2023–2025. In the European Union, broad EU‐level coverage coexists with limited national issuance. The paper contributes a common framework for comparing climate and nature policies and distinguishes EU‐level coverage from national policy development. The results show that the climate‐nature gap concerns not only adoption, but also where policies are used, how binding they are, and which level of authority issues them.

title: How the European Union Fell Out of Love With Open‐Source Software
abstract: This article explains why the European Commission diluted the 2004 European Interoperability Framework's provisions favoring open‐source software and open standards when it revised the framework in 2010. Using an extended Multiple Streams Framework with a technology stream, the study shows how pro‐openness policy entrepreneurs secured the 2004 provisions and why incumbent advocacy became more effective during revision. Drawing on annotated drafts and expert interviews, the study traces actors' lobbying strategies across the problem, politics, and policy streams and examines how technology‐stream developments altered the feasibility and political salience of competing solutions. The analysis shows how changing standards and licensing dynamics, incumbent advocacy, and declining political support for the earlier pro‐openness package enabled a new coupling around business‐model neutrality and licensing flexibility, diluting the 2004 provisions. Beyond the European case, the study informs debates on open‐source artificial intelligence and advances theory on institutional dynamics in regulatory governance.

title: Form Before Capability? AI Governance Adoption, Functional Capability, and the Limits of Index‐Based Evidence in the Global South
abstract: Governments across the developing world have adopted artificial intelligence governance instruments at high speed, though the relationship between formal adoption and the capability to operate those instruments remains poorly understood. This article asks whether the expansion of AI governance architecture across the Global South has been matched by the functional capabilities on which regulatory effectiveness depends, and what explains the answer. Drawing on panel data for 82 countries across five Global South regions and six waves of the Government AI Readiness Index, it reports that within the period of stable index architecture (2020–2024) measures of regulatory form rose by 20.3 points on a 0–100 scale while measures of functional capability rose by 0.4 points, a within‐country differential present in 90% of sample countries and surviving removal of the single step‐scored indicator of national strategy adoption. The pattern of the differential discriminates among explanations: formal adoption rose four times faster in states in the top quartile of administrative capacity than in the bottom quartile, where capability fell; the most aid‐dependent states adopted least; and the differential is unrelated to regime type. This is inconsistent with the view that legislation is simply quicker to produce than infrastructure and with the view that adoption is decoupled from performance for external audiences, and consistent with adoption conditioned on administrative capacity, in which capability in the weakest states erodes while capability in stronger states grows more slowly than the instruments that depend on it. Vietnam and India are developed as confirming and deviant cases. Cross‐national dispersion widened on both dimensions, and patterns that appear only when the 2025 wave is included cannot be separated from the redesign of the index in that year.

title: Power Lines: The Human Costs of American Energy in Transition By SanyaCarley and DavidKonisky, Chicago, IL : University of Chicago Press, 2025. 336 pp. $29.99 (paperback). ISBN : 978‐0‐22‐682562‐5
Collective intentionality in international relations: a reductionist view
abstract: The concept of collective intentionality has come to play an increasingly prominent role in the theoretical study of international relations (IR). In particular, scholars regularly treat two kinds of collectives – states and groups of states – as forming intentions and engaging in the joint pursuit of shared goals. In this piece, we intervene in the burgeoning IR debate on the ontology underlying this practice by making the case for a reductionist view of state intentions and joint interstate action. Drawing on Michael Bratman’s work on social ontology and original supporting arguments, we develop a sophisticated, non-summative reductionist account which overcomes many of the theoretical concerns that previously led scholars to reject reductionism as a viable ontological view within IR. Our account promises to advance both the empirical and normative study of international politics in several ways: it entails guidelines on how to study the origins of foreign policies and grand strategies; it lays the groundwork for novel views on interstate cooperation as it takes place in formats such as coalitions of the willing or security concerts; and it provides a promising framework for assessing collective moral responsibility and its relation to individual responsibility.

title: Deceit between Falshoods and Morality: Unpacking Audience Engagement with Disinformation
authors: Sabina Mihelj, Stefan Janjić, Hanna Orsolya Vincze, Andreea Alina Mogoş
abstract: Disinformation is customarily approached through an epistemic lens and defined with reference to intentionally false or misleading information. Yet, this approach struggles to account for how disinformation functions as a communicative practice that acquires meaning through audience interpretation and interaction. To develop a more comprehensive understanding, we draw on the analysis of eighteen focus groups conducted in 2025 in three countries that have been under increased scrutiny internationally due to their vulnerability to pro-Russian disinformation, but received limited attention in existing research: Poland, Romania and Serbia. Focusing on responses to examples of pro-Russian disinformation concerning the Russia-Ukraine war and LGBTQ+ rights, we show that participants judged claims not only based on credibility but also based on moral rightness, as well as engaged in contestations over the boundaries of legitimate controversy. Building on this evidence, we argue that disinformation not only creates uncertainty over how the world is but often invites contestation over how the world should be and over where the boundaries of legitimate public debate should lie. We conclude by reflecting on what these findings mean for scholarly research on disinformation, for counter-disinformation efforts, and for the way we understand the impact of disinformation on democracy.

title: The Promise of Multistakeholderism: Transnational Influence and Legitimacy at the Internet Governance Forum
abstract: Multistakeholderism is widely regarded as a means to ensure equal representation for stakeholders, promote democratic processes, and enable effective governance. Given the interconnected nature of the internet, much of global internet governance is influenced by multistakeholder approaches with a prominent role of transnational actors. This raises questions about the effects of transnational influence on the legitimacy of multistakeholder internet governance. Therefore, this article explores how transnational influence affects the input, throughput, and output legitimacy of the Internet Governance Forum (IGF), a key node within the internet governance ecosystem. The analysis combines qualitative content analysis of 600 statements made during cybersecurity governance debates at the IGF from 2016 to 2023 with 18 expert interviews. The findings reveal that transnational actors affect the IGF's legitimacy unevenly, producing both legitimacy gains and legitimacy deficits. Broad stakeholder participation contributes to high levels of input legitimacy, yet the prominence of specific transnational actors in panel discussions and policy contributions raises concerns regarding throughput legitimacy, reflecting persistent inequalities in access, resources, and visibility. While transnational actors' contributions significantly shape IGF policy outcomes, their influence is disproportionately concentrated among Global North actors. This article contributes to scholarship on transnational influence, the legitimacy of international organizations, and multistakeholderism.

title: Governing for Digital Resilience: Rethinking Inclusion for WSIS+20 and Beyond
authors: Audrey Yue, Jun Yu, Renae Sze Ming Loh
abstract: At the WSIS+20 juncture, this article asks what conditions enable individuals to participate meaningfully in digital life, and how governance arrangements should be assessed accordingly. Multistakeholder governance has distributed authority across actors, but not necessarily the capacity to shape or respond to digital conditions. We argue that assessing this gap today requires attention to the different forms of power through which these conditions are produced, and to individuals' experiences as evidence of how those governance conditions operate in practice. Building on socio‐ecological resilience theory and the capabilities approach, we reconceptualise digital resilience not as an individual trait but as a process shaped by governance conditions and by the substantive freedom people have to adapt, recover, and participate over time. We then introduce the DRIVE (Digital Resilience Indicators for Veritable Empowerment) framework, an indicator‐based diagnostic architecture spanning six drivers and five levels—individual, familial, communal, platform, and state—that shifts assessment from individual preparedness towards enabling conditions. Using fraudulent advertising on Meta's platforms as an illustration, we show how DRIVE can identify evidenced constraints, evidence gaps, and appropriate sites of remedy. Rather than offering a universal score, DRIVE provides a flexible architecture for context‐specific assessment of the conditions under which digital resilience develops.

title: Innovation and Competition on a Rugged Technological Landscape
authors: Steven Callander, Nicolas S. Lambert, Niko Matouschek
abstract: We integrate innovation into Hotelling's classic model of spatial competition. Potential entrants arrive sequentially and choose whether and where to innovate. They can innovate beyond the frontier, expanding the boundary of the market, or within a niche between incumbent products. Product quality is learned only after introduction, and uncertainty increases with novelty. Innovation on a rugged technological landscape is irregular, with frequent changes in direction and cycles between frontier and niche innovation. The ruggedness of the technological landscape itself deters innovation, generating fewer entrants, less product differentiation, narrower markets, and more intense competition than under certainty. (JEL D11, D21, D83, L11, L25, O31)

title: Recurring Auctions with Costly Entry: Theory and Evidence
abstract: Recurring auctions are widely used to sell durable assets, with follow-up auctions held for unsold items. We investigate such auctions theoretically and empirically. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that recurring auctions outperform single-round auctions when buyers face entry costs, enhancing efficiency and revenue due to sorted entry of potential buyers. Optimal reserve price sequences are characterized. Empirical findings from home foreclosure auctions in China reveal significant annual gains in efficiency (US$3.40 billion, 16.60 percent) and revenue (US$2.97 billion, 15.92 percent) using recurring auctions compared with single-round auctions. Implementing optimal reserve prices can further improve efficiency (3.35 percent) and revenue (3.06 percent). (JEL D44, D82, R31)

title: Learning in the Marriage Market: The Economics of Dating
authors: Yair Antler, Daniel Bird, Daniel Fershtman
abstract: This paper develops a search-and-matching model where potential partners can learn about their compatibility as a couple by spending time together (interpreted as dating). We show that a steady-state equilibrium exists and characterize its induced dating patterns. In equilibrium, highly attractive individuals are more selective. We derive conditions under which equilibria induce positive assortative matching and show that even when these conditions hold, the socially optimal outcome can exhibit negative assortative matching. Finally, the framework is applied to study the effect of recent advances in search technologies on dating patterns and the connection between dating and interracial segregation. (JEL C78, D83, J12)

title: Cognitive Ability and Perceived Disagreement in Learning
abstract: Do agents believe they agree more with others over time? This paper explores how individuals perceive the belief-updating behavior of others and the resulting disagreement in a sequential experiment with public information. We uncover a persistent gap in the perception of disagreement as a function of cognitive ability. Higher cognitive ability correlates with less perceived disagreement, although the average subject underestimates the extent of actual disagreement. Information about a partner's cognitive ability only impacts perceived disagreement when the partner has a low test score. Our findings highlight the roles of overconfidence and cognitive projection in shaping these perceptions. (JEL C91, D12, D83, D91)

title: Degree-Weighted Social Learning
authors: Chen Cheng, Xiao Han, Xin Tong, Yusheng Wu, Yiqing Xing
abstract: We study social learning in which agents weight neighbors' opinions differently based on their degrees, capturing situations in which agents place more trust in well-connected individuals or, conversely, discount their influence. We derive asymptotic properties of learning outcomes in large stochastic networks and analyze how the weighting rule affects societal wisdom and convergence speed. We find that assigning greater weight to higher-degree neighbors harms wisdom but has a non-monotonic effect on convergence speed, depending on the diversity of views within high- and low-degree groups, highlighting a potential trade-off between convergence speed and wisdom. (JEL D83, D85, Z13)

title: Land, Wealth, and Taxation
authors: Roberto Brunetti, Carl Gaigné, Fabien Moizeau
abstract: This paper examines the role of land in wealth dynamics and its consequences for efficiency and inequality. We focus on the interplay among agents’ bidding for location, mortgage market imperfections, and inheritance in a model in which agents leave to their heirs financial bequests and their housing wealth. The borrowing constraint generates a housing return premium and spatial wealth sorting, which translate into persistent wealth inequality. Since altruism and the borrowing constraint distort land price formation, we show that taxing land rent transmitted between generations is optimal. Land taxation cannot be disconnected from taxation on intergenerational wealth transfers. (JEL D31, D64, H71, Q24, R23, R31, R52)

title: Strategic Limit Orders and Intertemporal Price Dispersion
authors: Suman Banerjee, Ravi Jagannathan, Kai Wang
abstract: We study a two-period commodity market with competitive consumers and Cournot sellers. Without speculation, equilibrium is stationary. A storage-capable, strategically large speculator can profitably create deterministic intertemporal price dispersion using standard order types. A period-1 limit buy order flattens residual demand, induces higher output, and yields a low purchase price. With mandatory liquidation, resale remains below the no-speculation price but above the purchase price, so the speculator profits; consumers gain and sellers lose. With free disposal and a stop-loss, the period-2 price can exceed the benchmark, benefiting sellers but harming consumers. (JEL D43, G12, G14, G41, Q02)

title: Electoral Campaign Attacks: Theory and Evidence
abstract: This paper studies the determinants of electoral campaign attacks. We first propose a model to examine the main factors that influence candidates' decisions to attack. Our theoretical analysis yields a number of predictions that we test using information from “right of reply” lawsuits filed in Brazil. Our empirical analysis exploits a regression discontinuity design based on virtual ties between second- and third-place candidates to show that candidates with an electoral advantage are more likely to receive an attack. We then exploit another discontinuity to show that the patterns of campaign attacks differ significantly under single- and dual-ballot plurality systems. (JEL D72, D74, K16)

title: Competitive Bottlenecks and Platform Spillovers
abstract: We provide a general framework to analyze competition between oligopolistic platforms in competitive bottleneck settings, allowing for pricing and nonprice design choices by platforms, and post-participation buyer-seller decisions. We show that equilibrium choices by platforms are distorted against sellers’ interests in a way harmful to welfare (e.g., setting excessive commission fees), and that an increase in the number of competing platforms can exacerbate this distortion. We also characterize how buyer-side heterogeneity in interaction benefits, partial market coverage, platform asymmetry, and cross-platform spillovers further amplify or mitigate welfare distortions. Based on our findings, we discuss policy implications for mobile app platforms. (JEL D43, L13, L25, L96)

title: Competing Diffusions in a Social Network
authors: Arthur Campbell, C. Matthew Leister, Philip Ushchev, Yves Zenou
abstract: We develop a model of competing diffusions of goods on a social network. There are two types of goods and individuals: mass-market and niche-market. There is a unique stable steady state, and the adoption of a mass-market good is greater than its population share. Greater connectivity and homophily will concurrently increase the prevalence of niche-market goods. If there is a strategic agent who wants to promote a niche good, she will invest more in influencing activities than one promoting mass-market goods. When individuals choose their degree of homophily, niche-market individuals exhibit greater homophily than mass-market ones. (JEL D83, D85, L86, Z13)

title: Reputation and Competitive Selection
abstract: We demonstrate how selection in competitive markets can impede long-run reputational incentives. In our model, competent firms can exert costly effort to improve expected product quality, but inept firms cannot. With low entry barriers, we show competent firms cannot persistently exert effort, despite bounded memory. Such effort would cause consumers to select firms based on reputations for competence, eventually selecting a monopolist with an arbitrarily high reputation, which has no incentive for effort. More generally, reputation-based selection rules out long-run effort, which undermines the basis for such selection. Intermediate entry barriers provide stronger reputational incentives than low or high barriers. (JEL D21, D40, D82, L15)

title: The Perils of Overreaction
abstract: To study updating rules, we consider the problem of a malevolent principal screening an imperfectly Bayesian agent. We uncover a fundamental dichotomy between underreaction and overreaction to information. If, for some signal realization, the agent's updating rule produces a posterior that lies outside the convex hull of the Bayesian posteriors induced by the signal structure, she can be exploited by the principal without bound: Her ex ante expected loss can be made arbitrarily large. In contrast, an agent who underreacts—whose posterior after each signal realization lies between the prior and the corresponding Bayesian posterior—cannot be exploited at all. (JEL D82, D83)

title: Targeted Advertising in Elections
abstract: How does targeted advertising influence electoral outcomes? This paper presents a one-dimensional spatial model of voting in which a privately informed challenger persuades voters to support him over the status quo. I show that targeted advertising enables the challenger to persuade voters with opposing preferences and swing elections decided by such voters. Ex ante commitment power is unnecessary—the challenger succeeds by strategically revealing different pieces of verifiable information to different voters. Publicizing all political ads would mitigate the negative effects of targeted advertising and help voters collectively make the right choice. (JEL D72, D82, D83, M37)

title: Symmetric Equilibrium in Pre-auction Investment
abstract: We characterize the symmetric equilibria of a pre-auction game of investment in an internet ad auction environment. For a wide class of auction formats, we show a symmetric equilibrium exists for the pre-auction investment game, is essentially unique, and is the same for all auction formats in the class. We give sufficient conditions for the symmetric equilibrium to be in pure strategies and to achieve the efficient level of investment. Finally, we show comparative statics results with respect to a variety of parameters. (JEL D44, D82)

title: Optimal Procurement Design: A Reduced-Form Approach
abstract: Standard procurement models assume that the buyer knows the quality of the good at the time of procurement; however, in many settings, the quality is learned only long after the transaction. We study procurement problems in which the buyer's valuation of the supplied good depends directly on its quality, which is unverifiable and unobservable to the buyer. For a broad class of procurement problems, we identify procurement mechanisms maximizing any weighted average of the buyer's expected payoff and social surplus. The optimal mechanism can be implemented via an auction that restricts sellers to submitting bids within specific intervals. (JEL D44, D82, H57, L15)

title: Monopolistic Data Dumping
abstract: A profit-maximizing monopolist curates a database for users seeking to learn a parameter. There are two user types: “Nowcasters” wish to learn the parameter's current value, while “forecasters” target its long-run value. Data storage involves a constant marginal cost. The monopolist designs a menu of contracts described by fees and data-access levels. The profit-maximizing menu offers full access to historical data, while current data are fully provided to nowcasters but may be withheld from forecasters. Compared to the social optimum, the monopolist keeps too much historical data, keeps too little current data, and may store too much data overall. (JEL C53, C80, D42, L12, L86)

title: The Unintended Consequences of Academic Leniency
authors: A. Brooks Bowden, Viviana Rodriguez, Zach Weingarten
abstract: Education is widely recognized as the primary driver of human capital accumulation. However, policies designed to promote educational attainment often overlook students’ endogenous responses. This paper provides empirical evidence of the causal impact of relaxed academic standards on student effort and achievement. We find that academic leniency results in mechanical GPA increases, but significant reductions in effort among lower ability students based on lower attendance and lower numerical grades. These heterogeneous effects compound and exacerbate gaps in engagement and achievement throughout high school, ultimately worsening deficits in human capital accumulation as measured by ACT scores. (JEL H75, I21, I24, I28, J15)

title: Childhood Health Shocks and the Intergenerational Transmission of Inequality
authors: Tine M. Eriksen, Amanda P. Gaulke, Niels Skipper, Jannet Svensson, Peter R. Thingholm
abstract: This paper documents a socioeconomic gradient in adult labor market penalties stemming from a single chronic and treatable childhood health shock in a country with universal access to health care. Using childhood onset type 1 diabetes, Danish administrative registry data, and causal forests, we estimate substantial variation in the employment and earnings penalties at age 30. These penalties vary systematically with parental income and maternal educational attainment. Our findings help explain the income-health gradient and have important implications for policy discussions related to the design of health care systems. (JEL H51, I12, I13, I18, J16, J23, J31)

title: China’s Nationwide CO 2 Emissions Trading System: A General Equilibrium Assessment
authors: Lawrence H. Goulder, Xianling Long, Chenfei Qu, Da Zhang
abstract: China’s CO 2 emissions trading system, the world’s largest, aims to significantly reduce CO 2 emissions. The system is a tradable performance standard (TPS), differing from cap and trade (C&T). We provide a dynamic general equilibrium assessment that uniquely considers institutional and fiscal features of China that affect policy costs and distributional impacts. Key findings: The TPS’s environmental benefits exceed its costs by a factor of five or more. Interactions with the fiscal system reduce or eliminate the TPS’s cost disadvantage relative to C&T. Introducing auctioning as a complementary source of allowance supply can reduce costs by 30 percent. (JEL D58, O13, P28, Q54, Q58)

title: The Role of Race in the Legal Representation of Low-Income Defendants
abstract: Little is known about the role of race in the defense of low-income defendants by court-appointed attorneys. Exploiting the quasirandom assignment of court-appointed attorneys to cases, we test whether attorneys secure better deals for same-race defendants. Results indicate that while Black and White attorneys are similarly effective at representing White defendants, Black defendants who are represented by White rather than Black attorneys are 14–16 percent more likely to have their charges dismissed and 15–26 percent less likely to be incarcerated. Moreover, we find no evidence that having a different-race attorney increases the likelihood of reoffending in the future. (JEL H76, J15, K14, K42)

title: The Effect of Deactivating Facebook and Instagram on Users’ Emotional State
authors: Hunt Allcott, Matthew Gentzkow, Benjamin Wittenbrink, Winter Mason, Arjun Wilkins, Natalie Jomini Stroud, Joshua A. Tucker,
abstract: We estimate the effect of social media deactivation on users’ emotional state in two large randomized experiments before the 2020 US election. People who deactivated Facebook for the six weeks before the election reported a 0.060 standard deviation improvement in an index of happiness, depression, and anxiety, relative to controls who deactivated for just the first of those six weeks. People who deactivated Instagram for those six weeks reported a 0.041 standard deviation improvement relative to controls. Exploratory analysis suggests that the Facebook effect is driven by people over 35, while the Instagram effect is driven by women under 25. (JEL D12, D91, I31, J16, L82)

title: Identifying Tax Compliance from Variation in Tax Policy: Theory and Empirics
authors: Andrew Bibler, Laura Grigolon, Keith F. Teltser, Mark J. Tremblay
abstract: Governments increasingly use changes in tax rules to combat evasion. We develop a general approach to point-identify tax compliance along with supply and demand elasticities. Identification requires data on prices and quantities, variation in tax policy, and a demand or supply shifter. We illustrate our approach using data on Airbnb collection agreements, where taxes are enforced by shifting the statutory burden away from hosts and onto renters via the platform. We find that taxes are paid on roughly 0 to 1.6 percent of Airbnb transactions prior to enforcement. (JEL H25, H26, H71, K34, L83)

title: Impacts of Corporate Tax Cuts on Firms and Workers: Evidence from Small Businesses
abstract: This paper assesses the effects of corporate tax cuts on small firms and their workers. Following a reform in Quebec, Canada, firms receiving tax cuts expand and their workers’ earnings increase compared to workers and firms without tax cuts. We estimate that overall workers bear 35 percent of the tax burden, with larger incidence falling on those with ownership in the companies they work at, through increased profits. Additionally, workers across each tercile of the within-firm earnings distribution benefit from tax cuts, possibly because fair-wage concerns matter when after-tax profits rise due to close interactions among workers in small corporate environments. (JEL D22, H22, H25, J31, L25)

title: Prioritizing Benefit? How Low-Income Patients Respond to Prescription Cost Sharing
abstract: This paper measures how cost sharing impacts older low-income patients, exploiting a discontinuity in eligibility for a prescription drug subsidy for those who lose access to the Medicaid-linked program. Higher drug prices resulting from subsidy loss lead to a 40 percent reduction in prescription expenditures, driven by a 16 percent quantity reduction of prescriptions filled. Patients economize on purchases of higher-priced drugs, irrespective of their health benefits. For example, patients reduce insulin purchases by 35 percent. There is no evidence that cost sharing prompts switching from branded drugs to generics. This behavior suggests that cost sharing reduces prescription accessibility without enhancing cost-effectiveness. (JEL D24, I11, I18, I32, I38, L65)

title: Can You Erase the Mark of a Criminal Record? Labor Market Impacts of Criminal Record Remediation
authors: Amanda Agan, Andrew Garin, Dmitri Koustas, Alexandre Mas, Crystal S. Yang
abstract: We investigate whether removing a previously obtained criminal record improves employment outcomes. We estimate the causal impact of criminal record remediation laws that have been widely enacted with the goal of improving employment opportunities for millions of individuals with records. We find consistent evidence that removing an existing record does not improve labor market outcomes, on average. A notable exception is participation in gig work through online platforms, which often screen workers based on their records but not their employment histories. The evidence is consistent with records initially scarring labor market trajectories in a way that is difficult to undo later. (JEL H76, J22, J23, K14, K42, M51)

title: A Matter of Time? Measuring Effects of Public Schooling Expansions on Families
authors: Chloe R. Gibbs, Jocelyn Wikle, Riley Wilson
abstract: We leverage pronounced changes in the availability of public schooling for young children—through duration expansions to the kindergarten day—to better understand how an implicit childcare subsidy affects mothers and families. Exploiting full-day kindergarten variation across place and time from 1992 through 2022 and novel data on state-level policy changes, combined with a comparison of children of typical kindergarten-age to older children, we measure effects on parental labor supply and family childcare expenses. Full-day kindergarten expansions were responsible for as much as 24 percent of the growth in employment of mothers with kindergarten-age children in this time frame. (JEL H75, I21, J12, J13, J16, J22)

title: How Effective Are R&D Tax Incentives? Reconciling the Micro and Macro Evidence
authors: Silvia Appelt, Matěj Bajgar, Chiara Criscuolo, Fernando Galindo-Rueda
abstract: Recent firm-level studies find R&D tax incentives to be much more effective at stimulating firms’ R&D investment than aggregate analyses suggest. Based on a distributed analysis of official R&D survey and administrative tax relief microdata for 19 OECD countries, we show that two factors can reconcile these contrasting results. First, the limited uptake of R&D tax incentives in most countries makes aggregate studies underestimate the effectiveness of R&D tax incentives. Secondly, R&D tax incentives are (much) less effective for large and R&D-intensive firms, which account for a small share of R&D-performing firms but most aggregate R&D tax relief. (JEL D22, H25, H32, L25, O31)

title: The Pass-Through of Retail Crime
abstract: This paper shows retailers increase prices in response to organized retail crime. We match store-level crime data to scanner data from the universe of transactions for cannabis retailers in Washington state. Using quasi-experimental variation from robberies and burglaries, we find a 1.7–1.8 percent price increase at victimized stores and nearby competitors. This rise is not driven by short-to-medium-term demand changes but is consistent with crime-related cost shocks. Effects are larger for independent stores and less concentrated markets. We estimate crime imposes a 1 percent “hidden” unit tax on affected stores, implying $30.7 million in additional social costs, primarily borne by consumers. (JEL D22, H22, H76, K42, L81)

title: Trade Protection along Supply Chains
authors: Chad P. Bown, Paola Conconi, Aksel Erbahar, Lorenzo Trimarchi
abstract: We study the effects of trade protection along supply chains. We focus on temporary trade barriers against China, which has been the main target of US trade protection during the last decades. To deal with endogeneity concerns, we use an instrumental variable strategy, exploiting changes in the identity of swing states across presidential terms and heterogeneous exposure to these political shocks across industries. We find that politically motivated trade protection generates winners and losers: It fosters employment growth in protected industries but hampers employment growth in downstream industries. Our estimates imply a negative overall impact on US jobs. (JEL D72, F13, F14, L14, O19, P33)

title: Polluted IPOs
authors: Meng Miao, Wei Wang, Zhengyu Zuo
abstract: Chinese companies must undergo a review by a regulator-appointed committee before proceeding with initial public offerings (IPOs). We find that firms—particularly, politically unconnected ones—are more likely to pass this review on polluted days (i.e., with a high level of PM2.5). The effect appears driven by reduced cognitive capacity among reviewers, reflected in fewer and simpler questions raised during review sessions. Notably, firms approved on polluted days show no significant performance difference from other firms within three years after the IPO. The findings suggest that pollution-induced cognitive fatigue may paradoxically reduce distortions in a politically influenced approval process. (JEL D22, G24, G32, K22, P28, P31, Q52)

title: Inclusive Teaching: Spotting Social Isolation in the Classroom
authors: Sule Alan, Michela Carlana, Marinella Leone
abstract: We evaluate an intervention aimed at addressing social isolation in classrooms. The treatment provides teachers with their students’ social networks and information on developmental risks associated with social exclusion. Using friendship data and incentive-compatible measures, we find that the intervention reduces social isolation and antisocial behavior but does not increase prosocial behavior. Lower antisocial behavior enhances economic efficiency, reflected in higher average student payoffs and reduced inequality. Our findings highlight the personal and communal benefits of addressing social exclusion and antisocial peer dynamics in schools. (JEL D91, I21, I24, I28, J13, Z13)

title: On-Demand Assistance: Experimental Evidence from Indonesia
authors: Rema Hanna, Benjamin A. Olken, Sudarno Sumarto, Achmad Maulana, Vivi Alatas, Elan Satriawan
abstract: Given labor informality in developing countries, addressing employment shocks is challenging. We study Indonesia’s new approach for on-demand online applications for temporary cash assistance and online job training. Through 20 lotteries over two years, 11 million beneficiaries were selected. In nationwide representative surveys matched with administrative data, most beneficiaries report not receiving the assistance, with no detectable impact on employment or consumption. In contrast, survey data from applicants with working phones reveal high reported take-up and higher incomes. The results suggest that, while flexible, on-demand assistance has potential, design features that allow for flexibility could hinder receipt and, thus, impact. (JEL E21, E24, I38, J24, J46, O15)

title: Global arable land redistribution toward the tropics and drylands under human settlement expansion
authors: Lun Gao, Xiaoman Lu, Weston Anderson, Corey Lesk, Elise Mazur, Fred Stolle, Peter Potapov, Francesco N. Tubiello, Steffen Fritz, Jiafu Mao, Liangzhi You, Deepak Ray

title: Do felon voting rules affect criminal prosecutions?
abstract: Felon disenfranchisement laws can alter the composition of the electorate. Accordingly, we argue that in states with such laws, elected prosecutors may be tempted to assign felon status strategically. We test our argument using criminal case data from Virginia and leveraging a sudden policy change—unexpectedly announced by the Governor on April 22, 2016—enfranchising all felons upon completion of their prison or probation sentence. Using well-known racial differences in partisanship as a measure of likely political alignment, we show that the announcement corresponded to an increase in criminal charge severity and sentence length for defendants who were politically unaligned with their prosecutors, and a decrease for aligned defendants. Evidence suggests that these changes may have been partially motivated by partisan concerns in the lead-up to the 2016 federal elections.

title: Polity size and women’s representation: evidence from two large-scale boundary reforms
authors: Moa Frödin Gruneau, Jan Teorell, Kåre Vernby
abstract: Do larger polities hinder gender parity in elected office? We theorize that when populations grow faster than elected assemblies, a “seat congestion” effect intensifies competition for nominations, enabling men candidates to crowd out women. We test this argument using two nationwide natural experiments: Swedish municipal amalgamations in 1952 and 1973 that abruptly increased electorates. We track the effects in newly digitized historical panel data. Where electorate-per-seat ratios rose, growth in women’s representation slowed. Decomposition analyses show that expanding councils only partially offsets congestion. By identifying polity size as a systematic brake on descriptive representation, the study adds a demographic dimension to debates on institutional design and points to an overlooked cost of increasing jurisdictional size.

title: “Manifestly unlawful”: How US troops think about the duty to disobey illegal orders
authors: Charli Carpenter, Heather Kumove, Geraldine Santoso
abstract: US troops are required to disobey unlawful orders but obey lawful ones – yet social scientists know very little about how they draw that line or what drives the decision to actually disobey when it counts. We asked 818 active-duty American troops to define “manifestly unlawful orders” in their own words, as well as whether they would obey or disobey specific scenarios in which they might be asked to directly and intentionally target unarmed civilians. A majority of troops could provide clear examples of situations in which they would feel compelled to disobey orders. Of specific scenarios, over a third of US troops were prepared to disobey orders to target civilians, either with nuclear weapons or if asked to shoot civilian protesters. Controlling for gender, age, branch of service, party affiliation, voting behavior, rank, income, and education, we find simply thinking ahead about the concept of “manifestly unlawful orders” is the single biggest predictor of soldiers’ willingness to refuse to harm civilians.

title: Worth a try? The electoral consequences of symbolic legislation
authors: Nicole Huffman, John V. Kane, David L. Stack
abstract: With the US Congress increasingly gridlocked, fewer bills are becoming law. Nevertheless, members continue to engage in what we call “symbolic legislating”—that is, introducing legislation that has effectively no chance of securing enough votes to become law. Despite its prevalence, little is known about the electoral implications of sponsoring symbolic legislation. It is possible that voters reward their legislator’s efforts to move the status quo closer to their position even if it has no chance of becoming law. On the other hand, because symbolic legislation is doomed to fail, it may decrease a legislator’s perceived effectiveness and, thus, their political support. Alternatively, it is possible that sponsoring symbolic legislation has no impact beyond a cue of the politician’s position. In this Research Article, we test these competing hypotheses using a survey experiment. Our experimental results clearly demonstrate that, assuming shared party and issue position, sponsoring symbolic legislation is strongly rewarded. Moreover, the effect is even stronger among voters who are most likely to attend to this information in the real world and operates similarly across parties.

title: Exploring the Predictors and Outcomes of Perceived Algorithm Responsiveness in Social Media Feeds: Combining Longitudinal and Computational Methods
authors: Samuel Hardman Taylor, David M. Markowitz
abstract: Perceptions of how algorithms curate content are integral to how people use social media and its effects. Building on the algorithm responsiveness process, we explore whether perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR) was associated with the message cues of algorithmically curated content. We coupled longitudinal data from a 7-day, twice-daily diary survey with computational digital traces from Twitter (now X) to operationalize algorithmic message characteristics and to understand the antecedents and outcomes of PAR ( N = 10,337 tweets). Results suggested that message cues from algorithmic content in social feeds (i.e., closeness, popularity, valence, and format) were associated with perceived message personalization, but message personalization was the only message characteristic associated with PAR. PAR predicted feeling more connected to others on Twitter, along with message-level factors: closeness to the poster and message personalization. This work contributes to the algorithm responsiveness process, demonstrating that characteristics of algorithmically curated messages predict how individuals experience algorithms.

title: Do Experts Agree About Misinformation? Evidence From Three Annual Surveys
authors: Sacha Altay, Sebastián Valenzuela, Philip N. Howard
abstract: How much do experts on the information environment agree about the scale, spread, and effects of misinformation? We drew on three annual waves of the International Panel on the Information Environment expert survey to examine agreement with seven popular claims about misinformation (2023: N = 262; 2024: N = 413; 2025: N = 442; spanning 76 countries). Agreement varied widely across statements and was stable across waves. About 60% of experts agreed that falsehoods spread faster than the truth and that misinformation is widespread. About half agreed that misinformation has a substantial influence on behavior and that people readily believe what they see online; about 40% agreed that more people have become misinformed over time; and only 25% agreed that misinformation is primarily a social media problem. The surveys also revealed a persistent divide between experts who saw misinformation as widespread and consequential and those more skeptical, with sharpest disagreement on its behavioral impact and increase over time. In 2025, some experts distinguished between misperception prevalence and misinformation severity. Overall agreement varied by respondent background: agreement was higher among experts on developing countries than those on developed countries, higher among STEM researchers than social scientists, and lower among political scientists than communication scholars. Expert consensus on misinformation is partial, varies across claims and experts, and is shaped by geography and discipline.

title: Exclusion Forms Connection: The Presence of Immigrant Linked Fate Among Nonimmigrants
authors: Yoshira D. Macías Mejía, Lisa M. Sanchez
abstract: Immigrant linked fate is a new measure in the linked fate literature. In this study, we examine the predictors of immigrant linked fate, validate the measure of linked fate, and examine the role of immigrant linked fate in shaping immigration policy preferences among Latinos, Blacks, and Asians. We suggest that one must not be an immigrant to espouse immigrant linked fate. Therefore, “immigrant” linked fate has less to do with nativity and more to do with outsider status as the result of social exclusion. To test our hypotheses, we use the Collaborative Multiracial Post-Election Survey 2016 (CMPS) because it includes the measure of immigrant linked fate and a robust racial and ethnic group sample. The results suggest that Latinos, Blacks, and Asians have similar predictors of immigrant linked fate. We find immigrant linked fate is a distinct measure from racial linked fate and that immigrant linked fate predicts policy preferences.

title: Measuring White Identity
abstract: Scholars increasingly emphasize identity politics as a crucial factor influencing white political behavior, which is often conceptualized as a form of defensive solidarity. But does current measurement accurately capture this concept? This study reconsiders the measurement of white identity to more accurately reflect its conceptualization, distinguishing between identity and consciousness without imposing ideological interpretations of group membership. I develop and test adapted measures for white identity and consciousness, allowing for ideological variation, and find that existing measures disproportionately reflect whites who are racially conservative in part because of measurement. Testing the measures on support for Trump and affirmative action, I find that the effects of white identity are conditional on the ideological interpretation of group consciousness embedded in existing measures. This study challenges dominant assumptions about the inherent conservatism of white identity and contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of racial politics in the United States.

title: From presidents to parliaments? Party institutionalisation and constitutional reform in Armenia, Georgia, Moldova, and Ukraine
Gendered democratic resilience in Central and Eastern Europe: A comparative theoretical framework
The ethical trilemma in refugee protection: equity, sovereignty, autonomy
abstract: Disparities in the distribution of protection responsibilities are not just unequal but also highly inequitable. Such inequities can be expected to negatively impact both the scope and the quality of protection that states are willing to provide. The paper empirically demonstrates through the analysis of Europe’s responses to forced displacement from former Yugoslavia to Ukraine, that European states have struggled to effectively address the highly inequitable distribution of refugee responsibilities. EU policy makers find it easier to develop symbolic solidarity measures than to establish more substantive policy responses, i.e. they struggle to adopt the kind of cooperation that the public goods literature suggests is necessary to overcome collective action problems. This is due to the fact that substantive refugee solidarity initiatives, such as quota-based relocation, which are promising from an equity perspective pose fundamental challenges to both national sovereignty and the individual autonomy of protection seekers. How future EU policies will seek to address such solidarity dilemmas that lie at the heart of international refugee responsibility sharing efforts will tell us much about its commitment to effective refugee protection.

title: Learning by moving: Physical motion accelerates category learning
authors: Luke Rosedahl, Yuka Sasaki, Takeo Watanabe
abstract: Categorization is crucial for survival, helping animals forage, navigate, and avoid predators—all tasks involving movement. Yet, dominant theories of category learning treat it as a purely cognitive or perceptual process. Here, we challenge this view by demonstrating that physical movement can enhance category learning—but selectively. Using immersive virtual reality, we found that performing large actions, such as swinging a lightsaber, substantially improved learning of categories requiring integration of multiple cues (e.g., distinguishing aggressive from noncancerous lesions), while having minimal impact on categories involving independent evaluation of features (e.g., sorting by color and shape). This selective enhancement reveals a previously unrecognized motor contribution to categorization and may explain why prior studies missed it, opening avenues for optimizing training in critical categorization tasks.

title: Global socio-economic resilience to disasters
authors: Robin Middelanis, Bramka Arga Jafino, Ruth Hill, Minh Cong Nguyen, Stéphane Hallegatte
abstract: Most disaster risk assessments use asset damages as their central metric, often neglecting distributional impacts and affected people’s coping and recovery capacity. To address this, the concepts of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience—the ability to experience asset damages without a decline in well-being—have been proposed. Here we provide a global picture of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience using microsimulations. Across 132 countries, 1 dollar in damages causes well-being losses equivalent to a 2-dollar uniform national consumption drop. The poorest populations incur only 9% of damages but 33% of well-being losses. A 10% higher gross domestic product per capita is associated with a 1 percentage point resilience increase. Low-income countries experience 72% greater well-being losses per dollar of damages and need 92% longer to recover than high-income countries. Socio-economic and financial interventions can complement asset-focused policies, and targeting low-income populations usually yields higher well-being returns. Our results offer a starting point for a discussion on more comprehensive risk metrics and risk management policies for sustainable development.

title: Entertainment television and a wildlife documentary produce equal engagement but opposite conservation behavior
authors: Alexandra Boren, Diogo Veríssimo, Chase Alexander Niesner, Jiaying Zhao, Nicolas Ara, Alejandra Echeverri
abstract: Entertainment media reaches billions of people and shapes how they understand the natural world, yet its consequences for real conservation behavior remain largely untested.
