However, because the amount of labeled data needed varies across thematic analysis tasks, researchers and practitioners face uncertainty in the time, cost, and feasibility of applying scalable text analysis to planning research and practice. How much data needs to be labeled to achieve acceptable accuracy and how does this depend on the complexity of the task itself? This study proposes theory-informed models for measuring task complexity and defining the relationship between complexity and the number of labeled samples needed. Through the analysis of six thematic analysis tasks in 103 climate action plans (CAPs), we find that by only defining complexity from a codebook of phrases for a topic, akin to the process of manual thematic coding, it is possible to accurately predict the maximum attainable accuracy scores for any given training size and labeling a very small sample of data improves the accuracy of the prediction. This framework provides a way for urban researchers to determine the manual cost of extending a thematic coding task to larger scales before embarking on the process.

title: Partisan Bias in a Weak-Party System: Evidence from Kenya
authors: Jeremy Horowitz, Giacomo Lemoli, Kristin Grace Michelitch
abstract: Partyism---intergroup hostility along partisan lines---has been shown to be surprisingly strong relative to the underlying social divisions in several mature democracies. Less is known about partisan bias in weak-party systems where parties are less institutionalized and volatility is greater. This study examines partisan bias in Kenya, where parties are often made and remade in advance of each election. Results from survey-based measures and behavioral games show that partisan bias is substantively large both in absolute terms and in relation to measures of ethnic bias. The comparison with ethnic bias is particularly instructive given that Kenya is often described as a context where ethnicity is more central to politics than partisanship. We draw two conclusions. First, partyism can emerge in the absence of durable partisan identities, requiring more minimal conditions than implied in prior research. Second, explicitly priming partisan alignments can make core ethnic cleavages consequential in behavioral games.

title: ThSQCA: An R Package for Threshold-Sweep Qualitative Comparative Analysis
abstract: Qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) requires thresholds to construct sets from continuous scales, but a standard analysis is fixed to a single set of thresholds and does not directly reveal how the sufficiency structure changes when the target level of the outcome or the judgment criterion for a condition changes. This article introduces the R package ThSQCA, which uses the QCA package as its computational engine and provides a common workflow to run, aggregate, visualize, and report analyses that systematically vary the outcome threshold, the condition thresholds, or both. Using simulated data constructed for methodological illustration, we show that raising the target level of the outcome narrows the result from multiple sufficient paths to a single path (with lower consistency and higher coverage) and eventually yields no solution. We also show that varying the judgment criterion for a condition can make a solution disappear or produce a solution supported by very few cases. ThSQCA does not select an appropriate threshold automatically; it is a diagnostic workflow that clarifies the range over which a conclusion holds and the points at which it changes.

title: Transparency Is Not Enough: Political Identity and the Acceptance of AI-Generated Governance Information
abstract: Political transparency promotes accountability only if citizens are willing to accept the information provided. As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates the production and evaluation of public information, an important question is whether AI-generated political information remains subject to partisan filtering. We examine this question using an online survey experiment in Taiwan that varies two potential partisan cues surrounding an AI-generated legislative-performance evaluation: the partisan camp of the legislator receiving a favorable evaluation and the partisan alignment of the media outlet associated with the AI system. The results show that acceptance is strongly shaped by congruence with the favorably evaluated legislator. Respondents are more accepting when the legislator belongs to their own partisan camp and substantially less accepting when the legislator belongs to an opposing camp. By contrast, congruence with the media outlet associated with the AI system has no statistically significant effect. Further, prior generative-AI usage is positively associated with acceptance, but this association is significantly weaker when the favorably evaluated legislator is politically congruent with the respondent. These findings demonstrate that AI-mediated transparency does not eliminate partisan filtering and suggest that the partisan implications of AI-generated outputs may matter more than the political alignment of the institutions associated with their production.

title: Exploring the multidimensional impacts of child criminal exploitation: A scoping review
authors: Molly McCarthy, Mariel Mateo Pinones, Leanne Kelly
abstract: Background: Child criminal exploitation (CCE) is a serious form of childhood victimisation with potentially far-reaching consequences. However, evidence on its impacts remains fragmented. Objective: This scoping review synthesised research on the multidimensional impacts of CCE, explored common methodological approaches and identified knowledge gaps. Methods: Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we reviewed peer-reviewed studies published between 1990 and 2026 examining the impacts of CCE. Information on forms of exploitation, study characteristics, research designs and reported impacts was synthesised. Results: Sixty-five studies were included, which predominantly focussed on child sexual exploitation (83.1%). Most employed quantitative methodologies (78.5%), however there were relatively few longitudinal designs. Reported impacts spanned multiple dimensions, particularly mental health (n = 51), sexual and reproductive health (n = 25), re-victimisation (n = 23), criminalisation (n = 14), offending (n = 13), physical health (n = 13) and education (n = 13). Evidence of impacts from stronger observational designs was most prominent for criminalisation, re-victimisation and mental health. However, methodological limitations, inconsistent definitions and the predominance of sexual exploitation research constrained causal inference and generalisability of findings. Conclusions: CCE is associated with multidimensional impacts on children's lives. Nevertheless, the consequences of non-sexual forms of child exploitation remain poorly understood, and evidence that can establish the temporal ordering of impacts relative to exploitation is limited. Greater conceptual clarity and robust longitudinal research are needed to broaden our understanding of CCE impacts and to design effective policy responses and supports for affected children.

title: "Heaven without people is not worth going to”: refugee resettlement, time, and the institutionalization of family separation
abstract: We examine how resettlement as an institution, shaped by temporal opportunities and constraints over the lifespan, perpetuates refugee family separation. Based on seven years of qualitative research with households resettled through Canada’s Syrian Refugee Resettlement Initiative (SRRI), we show how the forced transition to nuclear family structures left almost no families arriving with extended households intact, leading to immediate negative impacts on self-reported well-being. Over time, we observed three outcomes of prolonged family separation. First, most families remained obstructed from reunification by the state in what we term unresolved protracted separation. Second, a minority secured partial negotiated reunification within the resettlement state through private sponsorship. Finally, another small group pursued next-generation reunification by arranging marriages for older children with left-behind kin outside the resettlement state. These responses reflect refugees’ adaptation to restrictive reunification policies amid declining family and humanitarian admissions and a growing privatization of immigration policy.

title: SciOps as Key Research Infrastructure: A decade of data to inform next steps for big science
authors: Anne E. Thessen, Catherine C. Saldutti, Melissa Haendel
abstract: Large, multi-institutional research programs now account for a substantial share of NIH-funded science, and Congress has called for greater accountability, transparency and coordination at the agency. Yet the operational demands of these programs fall mainly on principal investigators (PIs), who are selected and trained for scientific expertise. We examine the impacts of this mismatch using three sources of data. First, 232 participants in a large NIH-funded consortium answered an open-ended question about problems with collaboration and communication. Of 390 coded quotations, 337 named problems, and these mapped to all ten characteristics of effective teams described by NIH officers a decade earlier, most often to “effective leadership and management skills.” Second, we reviewed the PI eligibility policies of the 17 institutions that received the most NIH direct costs from 2014 to 2023. None requires demonstrated leadership, team facilitation or project-management competence. Third, we found that only 13 contact PIs each received more than $200 million in NIH direct costs over the same period; in some cases, their awards accounted for up to 85% of their institution’s NIH direct costs. If any of these PIs lacked operational or leadership expertise, it could have an outsized impact on their projects and on the people in their charge. To remedy these persistent problems, we propose SciOps: a small team of operational, financial, legal and communications experts with decision-making authority over operations, working alongside scientific leaders on large research programs. We further propose that NIH run a pre-registered pilot of SciOps with appropriate outcome measures. Such a pilot would show whether dedicated operational expertise improves how large-scale science runs.

title: The Organizational Infrastructure of Vigilante Violence: Evidence from India
abstract: Vigilante violence threatens order in many societies, but existing theories mostly focus on cases of state weakness. We argue that organizational infrastructure is an important enabling condition for vigilantes, even in relatively capable states and when violence appears to be spontaneous and mass-driven. Using an original dataset of 12,000 Hindu Nationalist schools—the most comprehensive measure of Hindu Nationalist organizational expansion in India to date—we show that vigilante attacks concentrate where nationalist organizations have the strongest, longest-lasting foundations, not in areas of contestation or new expansion. This pattern persists after accounting for state capacity, local demography, and the organization’s expansion strategy. Case evidence from three attacks shows that even apparently spontaneous violence depends on organizational capacity to recruit peripheral participants and stage violence as a public spectacle. Our findings identify organizational infrastructure as a source of variation in where vigilante violence occurs in capable states.

title: RESEARCH SYNTHESIS -- LLM-Based Simulations of Survey Responses: A Systematic Literature Review and Synthesis of Methods
authors: Hao Ting Chan, Dennis Assenmacher, Sebastian Stier, Claudia Wagner
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in survey research, including to predict, simulate, or impute responses. Despite a rapidly growing interest in applications to create synthetic survey data, the empirical evidence remains fragmented, with substantial variation in research objectives, model architectures, ``persona'' construction strategies, and validation practices. This paper presents a systematic review of 55 studies published between 2022 and 2025 that use LLMs to generate, predict, or impute responses in survey and related attitudinal or behavioral data. The results suggest that LLM-based survey simulation is best understood as a conditional, use-case-specific tool rather than a general substitute for traditional imputation methods and human respondents. We outline concrete steps toward a more coherent evaluation framework, including use-case-specific metric selection, relational alignment as a standard validity check, and greater transparency in model and design choices.

title: Private Data for Public Good: Facilitating Digital Footprint Data Sharing Between Business and Academia
authors: Romana Burgess, Laura Fryer, Anna Cupani, John Stuart, Michelle Morris, Anya Skatova
abstract: Digital Footprint data—routinely collected through everyday digital interactions such as online purchases, wearable devices, and app use—offer huge opportunities for societal benefit by providing large-scale, detailed insights into every day behaviours. Despite this potential, accessing these data remains challenging due to their proprietary and sensitive nature. This study draws on empirical evidence from a collaborative workshop, which brought together 50 multi-sector participants, including researchers, industry partners, government officials. Through facilitated discussions, participants examined the challenges and benefits of industry-academia partnerships in Digital Footprints research. Four key themes emerged: data access and entry to partnership, governance and infrastructure, incentives and value, and legitimacy and trust. By combining perspectives from both academics and industry, this work provides novel empirical insights into how multi-sector partnerships can maximise the value of Digital Footprint data for public good. Our key recommendations include the need for trusted intermediaries and internal company champions to facilitate collaboration; shared technical infrastructure, such as Trusted Research Environments and common protocols; emphasising societal benefit as a shared incentive alongside reputational gains for commercial partners; and recognising public trust as foundational to the long-term sustainability of Digital Footprints collaborations across stakeholders.

title: The Next Phase of Competency Assessment: A Research Roadmap for Social Work Licensure
abstract: Social work licensing examinations rely on a single response format: standardized multiple-choice items. The August 2026 Association of Social Work Boards (ASWB) redesign improved the blueprint, consolidating four content areas into three and reducing scored items from 150 to 110 on the basis of a 2024 practice analysis, but left the response format unchanged. This paper asks whether entry-level competence might be measured more validly through multiple assessment modalities, and argues that social work has raised this question since at least 2010 without producing evidence to answer it. It reviews that literature, including demonstrations that a language model selects keyed answers well above chance when the question stem is removed, and distinguishes licensure assessment from the educational competency assessment programs conduct under accreditation standards. It examines documented pass rate disparities, declines to treat format change as an equity remedy, and applies the same fairness questions to the multimodal formats it proposes, including measured racial disparities in automated speech recognition. It treats development cost and candidate volume as constraints rather than details. It concludes with a staged research design built to avoid the self-selection confound that would invalidate a candidate-choice pilot, and with an independent replication of the stem-removal analysis against the redesigned item bank, which needs no regulator cooperation and could begin immediately.

title: The Artificial Life of Politics: Synthetic Avatars and the Manufacture of Political Presence
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence allows political presence to be produced without the participation of those whose presence is displayed. Research has treated such media mainly as false records, or has studied AI presented as a political agent. This article examines a third phenomenon: AI that supplies the face, voice, or body through which human operators make a political appearance. It develops the concept of synthetic political avatars, analyzes them by referent, claimed basis of standing, accountability, and disclosure, and distinguishes four kinds of claims they make: to be a specific person, to be a typical member of a group, to speak for a group, and to present content as the work of a group. A layered comparison covers nineteen documented avatars in nine countries of the Global South between 2023 and 2026, set against contrast cases from other regions, institutional uses, and AI-driven candidacies. Across the core configurations, the cases reveal recurring gaps between synthetic presence and the strongest available basis of standing, while disclosure and authorization vary independently. Procedural governance of synthetic presence exists mainly in museums and foundations, not in electoral politics. The cases also support propositions about synthetic succession, the substitution of absent leaders, and the use of identity markers without participation. Generative AI lowers the cost of producing political presence without lowering the cost of authorizing or attributing it, and labeling, on its own, does not close that gap.

title: Female Empowerment and Network Value: The Contribution of Women’s Networks to Social Capital and Career Development among Female Leaders in Austria
abstract: This study, carried out within the framework of a Master Thesis, investigates the added value of women’s networks for female leaders in Austria, comparing them with mixed-gender networks and examining the role of mentoring as an empowerment instrument. Drawing on episodic qualitative guideline-based interviews with ten female executives (aged 27 to 65) from the public and private sectors, data were analyzed using Mayring’s qualitative content analysis with a predefined category system. The findings indicate that women’s networks primarily generate psychosocial capital by providing safe space, support, encouragement, and trust-based exchange. However, their direct connection to career success is limited. In comparison, mixed networks contribute more directly to career advancement through professional contacts and visibility. The results support a dual network strategy: women’s networks for self-efficacy and learning, and mixed networks for career acceleration and visibility. Women’s networks prove to be a valuable tool for women in leadership positions in Austria. However, to achieve sustainable change, it is essential to have male allies, structural adaptations and frameworks that systematically promote access, mentoring and inclusive networking.

title: Short-term rentals and residential rents: evidence from a regulation in Santa Monica
abstract: In recent years, there has been a significant increase in short-term rentals (STRs) facilitated by digital platforms such as Airbnb. This study evaluates the impacts of regulations imposed on these platforms, focusing on the Home-Sharing Ordinance implemented in Santa Monica, California. Using a Synthetic Control Method, the analysis finds that, two years after its implementation, the ordinance caused the number of Airbnb entire home listings to decrease by 60%. However, the study found no evidence that this regulation influenced long-term rental prices. Finally, suggestive evidence indicates that the ordinance did not increase the supply of houses allocated for long-term renters, potentially explaining its lack of impact on rents.

title: Visual presentation raises trust in election polls
authors: Elias Koch, Simon Munzert, Linus Hagemann, Hannah Rajski, Thomas Gschwend, Cornelius Erfort, Lukas Stoetzer
abstract: Election polls are arguably the most visible signals of public opinion in modern democracies, yet how the design of poll reports shapes their appeal, perceived credibility, and informational value has not been systematically studied. In a preregistered visual conjoint experiment conducted during the 2025 German federal election campaign, 22,658 voters evaluated poll reports varying across format, reference values, and technical information, in 160 possible designs. All visual formats were rated as more attractive and trustworthy than text-only reports. Trust gains were greatest among respondents with lower data and polling literacy and less accurate beliefs about current polling, whereas the appeal of visualization was greatest among the most literate. Disclosing the margin of error made reports less attractive without affecting trust, and no format made expectations about the election outcome more accurate. Text, the dominant format in poll coverage, is thus the least effective at fostering trust and accessibility.

title: Timing Matters: Nonlinear Exchange Rate Pass-Through and Inflation Dynamics in the Democratic Republic of Congo
authors: Christian P. Pinshi, Kevin M. Ngunza, Sungani Emmanuel
abstract: This paper investigates the exchange rate pass-through to inflation in the Democratic Republic of Congo within a nonlinear framework, using a Nonlinear Autoregressive Distributed Lag model. In a context marked by a recent transition toward an appreciation of the Congolese franc, the findings reveal the existence of a long-run relationship, as well as a significant asymmetry in the pass-through mechanism. Depreciations are transmitted rapidly and significantly to inflation, whereas appreciations generate slower and more delayed disinflationary effects. This asymmetry is primarily expressed in terms of timing rather than magnitude, highlighting an asymmetric price adjustment dynamic. The results also indicate a relatively high speed of adjustment toward the long-run equilibrium, although the structural influence of the exchange rate remains partial, confirming the multicausal nature of the inflationary process. From a monetary policy perspective, these findings suggest that exchange rate stabilization does not guarantee immediate disinflation and underscore the importance of managing expectations, particularly through the credibility and communication of the Central Bank of Congo. By providing an intertemporal perspective on exchange rate pass-through, this paper contributes to the literature by identifying a “timing rather than magnitude” asymmetry, and offers both analytical and operational implications for monetary policy conduct in emerging economies characterized by structural rigidities and high levels of dollarization.

title: Disproportionate Psychiatric Hospitalization of Black American Adults: A Replication Study
abstract: Disproportionate psychiatric hospitalization of Black Americans was found in a prior national study conducted with data collected during the COVID-19 pandemic (Barnes, 2026). The current study replicates the original study and reports on whether Black adults are hospitalized at a percentage higher than their population percentage and diagnostic differences between Black and White adults receiving services in state hospitals and other hospital inpatient settings. A subsample of adults ages 18 to 60 and older (N = 351,924) was drawn from the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s 2024 Mental health client-level data set. Univariate analysis found that the percentage of Blacks receiving services in state hospitals and other hospitals exceeded their percentage in the 2024 U.S. population (12%) by 17.2% and 9.2% respectively. Bivariate and regression analysis revealed an association between Black race and diagnoses of schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders in both hospital settings. The findings of the current study are similar to those of the original study.

title: Your health, their choice? The hidden inequalities of personalised health apps
authors: Ella Mintz-Davies, Charlotte Davies, Alexander Macgregor
abstract: The rapid expansion of personalised healthcare, often accompanied by claims of revolutionary improvements in wellbeing and disease prevention, warrants closer scrutiny. Personalised health apps have become increasingly prominent, especially since the COVID-19 pandemic, raising important social and ethical questions about accessibility, equity, and responsibility for health. Drawing on Michel Foucault’s theory of biopolitics and Deborah Lupton’s scholarship on digital health and self-tracking, this commentary argues that personalised health apps do not simply support self-care, but may individualise responsibility for prevention through digital forms of self-governance, with uneven consequences for different populations. In doing so, they raise questions about unequal opportunities to act on personalised health advice and the collective responsibilities of health promotion.

title: Returnees Reproducing Hegemony in the Digital Age: Off/Online Attitudes of the Western-born in Vietnam
abstract: **This paper has been accepted for publication in Southeast Asia: A Multidisciplinary Journal published by Emerald Publishing Limited** This paper examines how ethnically similar, yet culturally different ethnic return migrants use information communication technologies to reproduce and challenge Western hegemonies in their ancestral homeland. Drawing on 31 online in-depth interviews with 2nd and 2.5 generation Vietnamese living in Viet Nam, from 11 disparate Western countries, it explores the social-cultural, economic, and political (dis)advantages engendered within this hierarchically stratified, multiple-minority coethnic group. Employing Anibal Quijano’s concept of global coloniality, coethnic hierarchies are examined in the ethnic homeland. As such it asks, how are hierarchies among these coethnics played out off/online? To what extent are Western hegemonies reproduced off/online by Western-born ethnic return migrants and what are the tensions within this cohort in off/online groups?

title: Coalitions of the Willing: Designing Legislation for the Votes You Need
authors: Mike Cowburn, Sean M. Theriault, Steffen Hurka
abstract: Most laws require support from members of both parties. We test whether the coalition that enacts a bill leaves a signature in the scope and structure of the law it produces. In applying an enacting coalition typology to all public laws passed since 1947, we assess the impact on two measures of legislative design: the breadth of the legislation (versatility) and the clarity with which the law is written (precision). We find a clear relationship between the enacting coalition and the versatility of a law. Bipartisan laws are scoped more narrowly than more partisan legislation. For precision, we report null results. We complement our statistical approach with interviews of the House Office of the Legislative Counsel and two Senate legislative directors to better understand how these mechanisms function in practice. Our combined results suggest that the versatility of a law is a feature of the enacting coalition that is bargained over, whereas precision is contingent on the overall conditions within a given Congress.

title: Beyond Common Spaces: Contrastive Scaling for Cross-Survey Structural Comparison
abstract: This paper develops contrastive scaling as a framework for cross-survey structural comparisons. Whereas conventional bridging estimates a latent space shared across surveys, contrastive scaling identifies dimensions along which the organization of responses differs across them. We illustrate its utility using the UTokyo-Asahi Survey and a joint U.S.-U.K. dataset. The results show that, over time, Japanese voters have become increasingly divided over issues related to the status of the Jieitai (Japan Self-Defense Force), particularly in the structure of response distributions. In cross-national comparisons, U.S. and U.K. voters differ primarily along country-specific issue dimensions—such as attitudes toward Trump and Brexit—rather than along a common ideological axis. These findings demonstrate that contrastive scaling provides a complementary perspective on survey comparison by identifying dimensions of differential variation, offering a new lens for studying how public opinion is structured across contexts.

title: Global structure of the land by analytical regions: concentration and fragmentation
authors: Carlos Duarte, Carlos Andrés Salgado, Lina Diaz
abstract: In this text we will focus on what can be said with official and comparable sources about the structure of land ownership.

title: Analyzing the Impact of Explicit and Implicit Cognitive Constructs on NVIQ Test Performance
authors: Hope Sparks Lancaster, Alice Milne, Katherine Gordon, Samantha N. Emerson, Selin, Claire;claire.selin@boystown.org, Alicia Buttner
abstract: Purpose: Children with neurodevelopmental disorders historically have lower and more unstable nonverbal intelligence (NVIQ) scores compared to their typical peers. Herein, we posited that the intrinsic characteristics of the tests themselves, specifically the cognitive constructs they assess, might explain both the lower scores and variability across tests and over time. Using a qualitative approach, we examined how the explicit and implicit constructs are tapped on NVIQ tests and how these constructs compare across tests. Methods: Current editions of seven NVIQ tests were selected based on their use in clinic and research settings. Qualitative codes of constructs were determined through iterative development amongst SLPs and researchers. Codes focused on aspects of cognition most impacted in highly prevalent neurodevelopmental conditions, specifically attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and developmental language disorder. Results: We identified four main constructs across the tests which can impact measures of NVIQ in individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders. These constructs were attention, pattern learning, receptive language, and working memory. NVIQ tests differ qualitatively on these four constructs. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that the explicit and implicit constructs on NVIQ tests may explain why children with neurodevelopmental disorder have lower and more unstable NVIQ test scores compared to peers. We provide recommendations for use of NVIQ tests with neurodevelopmental disorder populations. We encourage SLPs and researchers to use our results to guide test interpretation and selection.

title: Enhancing Online Speech and Language Assessment: Item Development for the Remote Adult Language Experiment (ReAL-E) Tool
authors: Alicia Buttner, Hope Sparks Lancaster, Parks, Ryan M.;Ryan.Parks@boystown.org, Seth Bashford, Denis Fitzpatrick
abstract: Purpose: Recent technological advancements in psychology have yielded multiple unsupervised online tools for measuring cognitive skills. However, these tools do not measure key features of communication abilities in adults, such as productive speech or oral language. To address this gap, we developed the Remote Adult Language Experiment (ReAL-E) using a three-step approach that incorporates domain identification, expert evaluation, and piloting testing. Method: Step 1 focused on domain and task identification by collaborating with experts and reviewing the literature. Step 2 included two rounds of evaluation by content and lay experts to assess the initial tool design, identify areas for refinement, and solicit feedback for desired features. Step 3 involved piloting the tool in a sample of adults recruited online. Results: The ReAL-E tool adapted three speech planning and production tasks and four oral and written language tasks into online versions. Feedback from content and lay experts led to significant improvements, including enhanced task instructions, presentation modifications, and the incorporation of features to address potential confounds. Pilot testing demonstrated that adults perform within expected ranges, and five out of seven tasks had good to excellent preliminary reliability. Conclusion: The development of the ReAL-E tool contributes to the field by offering a scalable, efficient method for assessing a broad range of communication skills in adults, paving the way for future research and clinical applications in developmental communication disorders. Our study underscores the collaborative effort and innovative approach required for creating a digital assessment tool that promises to expand research capabilities and improve diagnostic processes in the discipline.

title: A meta-analysis of the relationship between speech and language development in children with nonsyndromic cleft palate with or without cleft lip
authors: Kari Lien, Paige Ellis, Nancy Scherer, Hope Sparks Lancaster
abstract: Objective: Children with nonsyndromic cleft palate with or without cleft lip (NSCP±L) are at risk for speech production and language delays. In typical development, a strong relationship exists between speech and expressive language development. However, our understanding of this relationship in children with NSCP±L is incomplete. Our objective was to determine the average correlation between consonant inventory and two expressive language skills in children with NSCP±L. Design: We used a random effects meta-analyses design. We identified articles for inclusion by searching PubMed, APA PsycINFO, and ERIC. Main Outcome Measures: Correlations between consonant inventory and (1) expressive vocabulary and (2) mean length of utterance (MLU). Result: Based on eight studies representing 187 children with NSCP±L, consonant inventory was positively correlated with expressive vocabulary size (k = 8, z = 0.74, SE = .16, p < 0.001, [0.424, 1.052]). Using data from four studies, representing 83 children with NSCP±L, consonant inventory had a positive nonsignificant correlation with MLU (k = 4, z = 0.513, SE = 0.293, p = 0.081, [-0.063, 1.088]). Conclusion: Our results support a connection between consonant inventory and expressive vocabulary size in children with NSCP±L across four languages. Small consonant inventories are often associated with expressive language delays.

title: What makes urban commons-public partnerships successful? Case studies in Switzerland on access to land
authors: Tianzhu Liu, Lilla Gurtner, Jean-David Gerber
abstract: Urban environments are facing growing ecological and social pressures associated with Urban commons initiatives potential to contribute to broader urban transformations may remain limited without institutional recognition. This study examines the mechanisms through which partnerships between municipalities and UCIs, termed as public-commons partnerships (PCPs), form around the governance of land-related urban resources. Drawing on 24 semi-structured interviews and 118 questionnaire responses from UCI representatives in Switzerland, we identify four categories of PCPs: enduring and mutual-recognition-based partnership, sustained yet non-dependent partnership, temporary and conditional partnership, and limited or absent partnership. Partnerships emerge when UCIs align with municipal objectives by advancing policy goals, resonating with political priorities, or strengthening policy implementation by same time, municipalities mobilize publicly owned land through diverse property-right institutional recognition and visibility while promoting urban resource governance that prioritizes collective use value, solidarity, and ecological stewardship. We argue that authorities mobilize public resources and regulatory capacities, while commons organizations contribute grassroots innovation, collective self-governance, and social more inclusive and ecologically oriented governance on urban environments.

title: Work or Study? Post-16 Pathways, Degree Attainment and Adult Life at 32
authors: Ingrid Schoon, Anna Yong, Andrew Jenkins
abstract: Progressing through education and into secure employment is central to young adults’ wellbeing and long-term life chances. Using longitudinal data, this study examines how different post-16 educational and employment pathways shape labour market and wider life outcomes by age 32. Building on earlier research on post-16 transitions, we classify young people according to their activities between ages 17 and 20 and whether they attained a degree by age 32, distinguishing routes that lead to similar destinations through different trajectories. We investigate the factors associated with pathway membership and assess their consequences for employment, earnings, job quality, home ownership, life satisfaction, and psychological distress. The findings show that transitions from education to work are diverse rather than linear, and are strongly shaped by prior attainment, socioeconomic background, family expectations, and available resources. These pathways have lasting implications for outcomes in adulthood. While the traditional academic route is associated with the highest economic returns, vocational and work-based pathways can also support successful transitions, particularly where they provide opportunities for continued learning and progression. The greatest divide is not between university and non-university routes, but between pathways characterised by sustained engagement and those marked by educational or labour market disengagement. In addition, there are substantial gender inequalities in employment, working hours, and pay by age 32. The findings highlight the importance of reducing educational inequalities, preventing disengagement in the late teens, and supporting progression through high-quality vocational, work-based, and academic pathways. Policy should recognise diverse routes into adulthood and ensure equitable access to opportunities for learning, employment, and advancement.

title: Another Empty Promise of Grade Retention? Peer Effects of Classmate Retention
abstract: Grade retention is a common but costly educational practice and studies have repeatedly shown that, in many contexts, it offers no academic benefit to retained students. A remaining justification for its continued use is the presumed benefit for the promoted peers from whose class the retained student was removed. This study tests that assumption using longitudinal data from the German National Educational Panel Study (NEPS) and a difference-in-differences approach, focusing on grades and competencies from Grades 1 to 9. Results predominantly yield null findings, with a small positive effect on mathematics grades in lower secondary education (0.08–0.09 SD) as the only exception. Overall, our findings do not provide support for presumed peer benefits as a justification for grade retention.

title: A Fatigued Frontline: Psychological Burnout and Coping Mechanisms in Indian Policing
abstract: This paper examines the structural root causes of police burnout and inaction in India, moving beyond the individualistic reasons to analyse policing as a product of systemic strain. The aim is to understand the psychological strain caused by chronic structural pressures and how they end up affecting the discretion and coping behaviours of frontline police personnel. The paper relies on secondary data collection, drawing its empirical findings from the Status of Policing in India Report (SPIR) 2019 and thematically analyses the findings through the lenses of street-level bureaucracy (Lipsky, 1980), and ways of coping (Tummers et al., 2015), while internally extending the concept of administrative burdens (Moynihan et al., 2015) to the street-level bureaucrats. The analysis reveals that chronic overwork, acute resource scarcity, political interference, and continuous public scrutiny create profound institutional insecurities and occupational burnout among the police officials. Lastly, the paper demonstrates that these pressures force the frontline officers to experience high psychological distress, leading them to often resort to defensive behavioural adaptations that impair policing outcomes in the country.

title: Constructing Measures in the Social Sciences: Best Practices and Common Pitfalls
authors: Piotr Koc, Zoe Greer, Lena Roemer, Matthias Roth, Julian Urban
abstract: Social scientists have long had access to sophisticated measurement models, but the instruments those models evaluate often receive far less care than the models themselves. Our aim is to close that gap by providing practical guidance for constructing valid self-report measures of latent constructs in sociology. We first establish a common terminology and an ideal four-phase construction process: defining the construct, developing an initial draft of the measure, empirical evaluation and iterative revision, and validation in an independent sample. We then identify six pitfalls that recur in applied work: imprecise construct definitions; conflating formative and reflective specifications; misuse of factor analysis, where global fit indices are treated as a summary verdict on scale quality; binary interpretations of measurement invariance tests; the neglected validation of single-item measures; and inattention to item-response quality. For each, we discuss the phases at which it arises, the consequences for substantive conclusions, and potential remedies. Throughout, political trust serves as a running example.

title: From Textbook Error to Moral Panic: Legitimation and Blame in Sri Lankan News Discourse on the Grade 6 English Module
abstract: In December 2025 a link to a website used for finding same-sex partners was found inside a Grade 6 English textbook produced by Sri Lanka’s National Institute of Education. What began as a printing error soon became a national political crisis, and the news coverage of it split along political lines. This study asks how two opposing news articles report the same event, and what their language choices show about power and ideology. It uses Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA), based on Fairclough’s three-dimensional model and van Dijk’s socio-cognitive approach, along with analysis of transitivity, presupposition, deixis, social actors, and mystification. Two publicly available articles were analysed. The first article uses conservative Buddhist nationalist language. Through passive sentences, an ‘us and them’ divide, and unargued assumptions, it frames the error as a moral conspiracy, sidelines the government, and gives no voice to LGBT people. The second article takes a left-progressive view. It defends the government’s response, compares the attacks on the Prime Minister to those faced by other women leaders, and builds a civic rather than culturally narrow idea of the nation, while avoiding naming the politicians behind the opposition campaign. Neither article simply reports the event; both take part in Sri Lanka’s wider political struggle after the 2024 election. The issue became politically powerful because negative attitudes to homosexuality are tied to religious and cultural identity. The study shows how everyday language choices carry competing ideologies in the news media. Keywords: Critical discourse analysis; media representation; ideology; Buddhist nationalism; Sri Lanka

title: Self-Making, Solidarity and the Sacred in Black Cuban Choreo/Geographies
abstract: Maya J. Berry’s book Defending Rumba in Havana: The Sacred and the Black Corporeal Undercommons brings Black Cubans’ sacred self-making, solidarity, and kinship practices into sharp relief. Her book explores not only how Cuban descendants of the formerly enslaved navigate longstanding and interlocking racial, gendered, and economic inequalities, but also Black Cubans’ aspirations beyond the political apertures of revolutionary statehood. Although rumba – popular depictions of which divorce the social dance event (20) from its religious roots – takes center stage, this is not a book about rumba. Rather, as Berry herself notes in the introduction, her research attends to what rumba as spiritual devotion and creative Black choreography reveals about the moves, struggles, and lifeworlds of its practitioners and those they claim as family.

title: Connections, reciprocity and wonder: Descriptions of meaningful experiences in nature reveal benefits for humans and environments in Australia
authors: Mae Woodruff, Kate Sollis, Usitha Rajeevan, Amber CY Tsai, Marcus Morse, Pauline Marsh, Emily Flies
abstract: 1. Having ‘meaningful’ experiences in nature – those that shape the way an individual views their relationship with nature – has been highlighted as one important way for people to deepen their connection with nature. 2. This mixed-methods study draws on a survey conducted across Australia in 2023 to better understand how people describe their meaningful experiences in nature and how meaningful experiences are associated with nature connection, wellbeing, and pro-environmental behaviours. 3. Through responses to the open-ended question: ‘Think of a meaningful experience you have had that shaped the way you think about ‘nature?’, we identified five themes: Formative childhood experiences; Connection with self, others and place; Giving back to nature; Stress relief and health benefits; and Wonder at the ‘bigness’ of nature. 4. Quantitative analysis found that providing a response to the meaningful-experience question was significantly associated with human-nature connection, life satisfaction (but only when human-nature connection was not controlled for), and three pro-environmental behaviours: advocacy behaviours, consumer-conscious behaviours, and conservation activities. The associations between reporting a meaningful experience and undertaking advocacy and conservation behaviours remained significant after human-nature connection was controlled for. 5. These associative findings have policy relevance, including supporting access to green space, opportunities for children to spend time in nature, and participation in environmental conservation. 6. Meaningful nature experiences were described as connecting people with themselves, others, and local places. Reporting such an experience was also associated with selected wellbeing and environmental outcomes.

title: Contact infrastructure and the wall: how international students' host-world affiliation is produced and bounded in Japan
abstract: International students' host-language use and social integration are usually explained by proficiency or national origin. This study argues that host-world affiliation is produced by contact infrastructure: the repeated, low-stakes occasions for contact that institutions and living arrangements provide. A wall of host reticence, produced by both sides, bounds it. The COVID-era withdrawal of these occasions is read as a revelatory rupture that made them visible by removing them. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design drew on a survey of international students (N = 176) and 39 interviews with 40 international students at one national research university in Japan. Four domestic students were interviewed as a labelled host-side comparison. Choice of the Japanese survey form indexed host-language orientation. Origin dominated that choice, while contact-type indicators were weak. The interviews explain the pattern. Affiliation followed the occasions for contact. When the pandemic removed them, reported loss largely tracked how much a student's world had rested on them. One of the 40 cases ran against this. Host and international students placed the campus boundary in the same location: in reticence and missing shared ground, not hostility. Participants described the wider society, by contrast, as hostile through housing, policing, and hiring. Nationality worked as a marker read from outside, not as a driver of conduct. The lever for belonging is the design of contact occasions, not language instruction alone.

title: Accounting for migrant definitions improves global migration modeling
authors: Danial Schirojan, Kristina Petrova, Maarten Vink, Karim Zantout
abstract: Reliable estimates of international migrant populations matter for migration policy, social cohesion, and integration. Most countries define migrants as foreign-born population, but about one in five defines them by citizenship. Under the citizenship definition, migrants are foreign residents who exit the migrant stock by acquiring the host country's citizenship. Existing migration models apply the country-of-birth definition to all countries due to data availability and reduced modeling complexity. We present a stochastic model that consistently applies the migrant definition of each country and represents citizenship acquisition as a probabilistic process based on legal residence requirements. Across 192 countries from 1990 to 2020, we find that accounting for migrant definitions improves the agreement of simulation results with UN reported migrant stocks. The normalized error against reported stocks decreases from 35.1% to 23.0% in Africa and from 18.1% to 13.6% in Asia, the two world regions where the citizenship-based migrant definition is most common. In lower-middle- and upper-middle-income destinations, the 95% prediction intervals cover the reported stocks in all reference years. Results in regions that apply a country-of-birth migrant definition remain essentially unchanged. Where reported figures are available, estimated citizenship acquisitions are plausibly represented within our model. Our results show that migrant definitions, and the citizenship laws behind them, shape the dynamics of migrant populations and not only how these populations are counted. The approach is transferable to other global migration models and can be refined as citizenship acquisition data become available for non-OECD countries.

title: Bypass, repurpose, weaken: a mechanism-based typology of niche strategies for niche actors under regime lock-in, illustrated through electric motorcycle adoption in Kenya
authors: Marcel Kempers, Linda Kamp, Gideon Ndubuisi
abstract: Sustainability transitions scholarship has developed two largely parallel analytical vocabularies: one explaining how incumbent regimes become locked in, the other how niche actors respond. This paper connects them through a framework of regime lock-in profile- strategy alignment. Nested within the Multi-Level Perspective, it characterizes regime lock-ins by tractability, materiality, coordination requirement, and coupling intensity, with regime coherence as a context-level modifier; and then introduces bypass-repurpose-weaken (BRW) typology that classifies niche strategies by the functional mechanism through which they engage regime lock-ins based on their structural profiles. A six-step operational protocol is further proposed, and the framework’s central proposition is empirically illustrated through an embedded case study of Roam, an electric motorcycle manufacturer in Kenya's boda boda sector. The case provides pattern-consistent support for the proposition: bypass clusters around material, tractable lock-ins; weaken around less material, tractable lock-ins; and repurpose where existing regime elements remain redirectable. The resulting pathway is characterised as bounded leapfrogging. Portability across regime configurations is specified analytically, while comparative testing remains necessary before prescriptive claims can be validated.

title: Income Volatility and Parenting Styles during Hard Times
abstract: Parenting styles are often intervened upon to mitigate disparities in children’s well-being, with the focus of scholarly and public debates resting on lower-income mothers. Although differences in parenting across the income distribution are well-established, the extent to which income itself might be one of the motors of such differences is disputed. Little attention has been paid to income volatility, in particular, despite its secular rise, recent salience, and the links between volatility and parenting drawn by theories across the social and developmental sciences. I thus investigate if and how income volatility affects parenting styles, relying on data from the UK Household Longitudinal Study (UKHLS, 2009-2022). Based on a variety of strategies to address measured and unmeasured confounding, I find that parenting styles are especially responsive to volatility among parents with household incomes above the median at baseline. For higher-income mothers, household and labour income instability are associated with lower warmth scores, whereas instability driven by household (benefit) income gains is associated with higher harshness and permissiveness scores. Differently, mothers with lower incomes score lower on harsh and permissive scales when experiencing benefit income gains. Fathers are especially affected by labour income volatility, with earnings losses leading to lower warmth scores among higher-income fathers, whereas the opposite is true for those with lower incomes. Findings shed light on how theories, public debates, and policies could be re-tailored to address the consequences of volatility on family life.

title: Finance in the Wake of Growth: Evidence from the Democratic Republic of Congo
abstract: This study revisits the finance–growth nexus in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), a highly dollarized economy characterized by shallow financial intermediation and limited access to credit. Using a Granger causality framework, the analysis examines the direction of causality between financial development and economic growth. The results provide little support for the Supply-Leading Hypothesis: private sector credit and monetary depth do not Granger-cause economic growth. Conversely, economic growth significantly Granger-causes private sector credit, providing evidence in favor of the Demand-Following Hypothesis. These findings suggest that, at the current stage of development, the Congolese financial system remains more responsive to real economic expansion than capable of independently driving it. From a development-finance perspective, the results imply that financial deepening alone may be insufficient to generate sustainable growth without complementary improvements in productive investment, infrastructure, human capital, institutional quality, innovation, and financial inclusion. The long-term policy challenge is therefore to foster a transition from a Demand-Following regime toward a Feedback regime in which financial development and economic growth become mutually reinforcing.

title: Private Equity Ownership and the Selective Deterioration of Quality in Childcare
abstract: Private equity (PE) ownership has expanded rapidly into socially consequential service sectors, raising concerns about its effects on service quality. Yet existing research has paid less attention to why some dimensions of quality deteriorate under PE ownership while others remain protected. We argue that PE’s distinctive financial pressures, short investment horizon, and managerial capacities encourage organizations to prioritize dimensions of quality that are visible and salient to consumers while allowing less visible dimensions to deteriorate, including dimensions that are observable to regulators. We test this argument using an original longitudinal dataset of 13,933 licensed childcare centers in Texas between 2010 and 2024. Two-way fixed-effects and event-study analyses show that PE acquisition is followed by substantial increases in regulatory violations, including serious violations. However, deterioration is selective: violations related to frontline staffing and caregiving capacity, child safety, facility maintenance, and procedural compliance increase, while staff qualifications and learning activities remain comparatively protected. These patterns persist when comparisons are restricted to other for-profit providers and even to for-profit chains. Our findings suggest that the consequences of financialized ownership for service quality depend, at least in part, on the relative visibility and salience of different dimensions of organizational performance to external audiences.

title: Delivering well-located dwellings: opportunities and challenges
authors: Rachel Ong, Steven Rowley, Piret Veeroja, Christopher Phelps, Stephen Glackin, Megan Robinson
abstract: This report delivers a comprehensive evidence base to inform the delivery of new dwelling supply in well-located areas in Australia and sheds light on the barriers holding back affordable developments in these locations. This research provides new evidence to help deliver the National Housing Accord’s target of 1.2 million new, well-located homes over five years from mid-2024. To date, most attention has been on the quantity aspect of the Accord target; this research focuses on the objective of delivering new housing in good locations. It identifies barriers and uncertainties holding back development, and what governments can do to speed up building in well-located areas.

title: Algorithmic Alertness and Imprinted Exits: Artificial Intelligence, Founder Characteristics, Opportunity Recognition, and Exit in South America
authors: Gabriel da Silva, Mateo González, Kavin Alves Santos, Sofía Quispe
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how new ventures are conceived, built, and ultimately exited, yet most theorizing about these shifts has been developed in North American and European settings where capital markets are deep and institutions comparatively stable. This essay develops a conceptual framework that links founder characteristics, AI-enabled opportunity recognition, and entrepreneurial exit in South America, a region marked by institutional voids, concentrated family ownership, rapid consumer adoption of AI, and thin, contracting equity markets. Drawing on upper echelons and imprinting theories, the cognitive literature on opportunity recognition, and an emerging view of AI as an entrepreneurial actor rather than a passive tool, we argue that AI does not so much substitute for founder characteristics as re-weight them. Algorithmic search lowers the cost of identifying opportunities but raises the premium on founder judgment, entrepreneurial drive, and political skill, which govern whether AI-surfaced opportunities can be legitimized and exploited where formal institutions are weak. At the exit stage, founder imprints formed under the region's recurrent macroeconomic crises shape not only whether founders sell or list, but whether they later reverse a public listing altogether, a pattern currently visible in the wave of delistings on Brazil's B3. The essay advances six propositions and outlines an agenda for research on AI-augmented entrepreneurship in emerging economies.

title: Constraints and Strategic Enhancement of Conflict Tracking Mechanisms for Effective Policing in FCT Abuja, Nigeria
authors: Basil O. Ibebunjo, Lydia Abumere Ozoemena
abstract: This study examined the constraints and strategic enhancement of conflict tracking mechanisms for effective policing in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, Nigeria. Specifically, it investigated the significant challenges hindering the effective implementation of conflict tracking mechanisms in the FCT Police Command and examined strategies that can be adopted to improve conflict tracking mechanisms for more effective policing in Abuja. The study was anchored on Situational Crime Prevention Theory (SCPT). A mixed-methods research design was adopted, integrating quantitative and qualitative approaches. Data were obtained from 389 valid questionnaires and qualitative interviews with relevant police personnel, community stakeholders, and other key informants. Findings revealed that the effective implementation of conflict tracking mechanisms is constrained by reliance on informal and reactive reporting channels, weak integration of digital communication platforms, limited institutional collaboration, inadequate technological infrastructure, and limited application of advanced analytical tools such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and crime mapping. The study further found that improved utilisation of conflict tracking information, integration of conflict data into patrol strategies and deployment, regular analysis of conflict indicators, enhanced personnel training, and stronger institutional collaboration constitute important strategies for improving conflict tracking and policing effectiveness. Qualitative findings reinforced these results, highlighting weaknesses in technological infrastructure, data integration, personnel capacity, and systematic information-sharing arrangements. The study concludes that strengthening conflict tracking requires a shift from largely informal and reactive practices towards more systematic, integrated, and proactive approaches to policing. It recommends an integrated conflict tracking framework, continuous capacity building for police personnel, and stronger collaboration among the police, community stakeholders, and civil society organisations through formalised early warning and information-sharing networks.

title: Where Work Is Moving Occupations, Academic Programs and Places in the 2035 AI Workforce Scenario: A Roadmap for Higher Education
abstract: The McKinsey Global Institute (MGI) estimates that, by 2035, automation could reduce U.S. labor demand by about a fifth of current work hours, while broader growth creates more jobs than automation removes. About 11 million workers may need to change occupations in the next decade. Colleges and universities plan programs years ahead, so they need to know what this scenario means for the programs they offer and the places they serve. We translate the MGI scenario into estimates for 830 detailed occupations, 1,432 academic program families at four award levels, and 530 metropolitan and nonmetropolitan areas. A task-level model of AI adoption, built from language-model exposure, observed AI success and review time, the cost of errors and governance, distributes MGI's totals across occupations. We also report the model's independent estimate and explain where and why it differs from MGI. Almost no occupation disappears: one falls by more than half and 62 fall by 20–50%. About 9.5 million jobs are in occupations that decline, almost half of them in office and administrative support. Program risk sits below the bachelor's degree. About 8% of certificate and 7% of associate completions are in programs whose graduates' occupations shrink by 10% or more, while 48% of certificates and 32% of associate degrees are in programs whose fields grow by 10% or more. At the bachelor's and graduate levels demand is broadly stable, but AI is expected to adopt or augment more than half of graduates' work hours, so the task is curriculum reinvention rather than closure. The need to change jobs is greatest in rural, agricultural and lower-wage areas; the wages at stake are greatest in high-wage hubs. We set out a roadmap for investment, reinvention, consolidation and review.

title: The First European Housing Project for Older Turkish Migrants in Haarlem, the Netherlands, and Its Lasting Legacies (1993–2008)
abstract: This article examines the first housing initiative for older Turkish migrants in Haarlem, the Netherlands, and its residential, policy-related and institutional legacies between 1993 and 2008. Emerging during the transition from temporary labour migration to permanent settlement, the initiative addressed growing concerns about migrant ageing, housing and welfare in Western Europe. Employing a qualitative historical case-study approach, the research draws on original archival correspondence, contemporary housing studies, governmental and architectural records, newspaper reports and supplementary historical testimony. The analysis focuses on three interconnected dimensions: long-term housing outcomes, changing policy perspectives on migrant ageing and the emergence of representative organisations. The findings document cooperation among European, national, provincial and municipal institutions, the presentation of the “Bizim Ev” research to Minister Hedy d’Ancona in 1993 and the development of differentiated housing programmes. Although the proposed residential complex at Prof. Boumanstraat was never constructed, its underlying housing objectives were subsequently reflected in a DP6-designed development completed in 2008. The initiative also helped bring the circumstances of ageing migrants into Dutch housing and welfare discussions, while its organisational experience contributed to the establishment of the Turkish-Islamic Elderly Union (TISBO) in 1993 and the Netherlands Islamic Elderly Union (NISBO) in 1995. The study illustrates how an early migrant housing initiative generated enduring residential, policy-related and institutional legacies beyond its original implementation period.

title: The Dialogic Paradox Across Platforms: Media Richness, Sentiment, and Phase-Dependent Engagement on Twitter During the COVID-19 Delta Rebound
authors: Abdallah Sayed Ali Essa, Sergey V. Kovalchuk
abstract: Background. Crisis communication on social media during pandemic rebound periods remains under-studied, and two competing frameworks — Media Richness Theory (MRT) and Dialogic Communication Theory (DCT) — offer divergent predictions about which content features drive audience engagement under acute uncertainty. Recent evidence from Chinese government microblogs (Zhang et al., 2022) suggests dialogic markers may reduce rather than enhance engagement during rebound periods, contrary to DCT's direct prediction, but no comparable evidence has been reported for Western platforms. Objective. To identify which content features of COVID-19 vaccine-related tweets predicted audience engagement during the Delta variant rebound of July–September 2021, test whether these effects hold across sentiment operationalizations and pandemic phases, and compare the resulting patterns with prior Weibo-based findings. Methods. We analyzed 71,845 unique vaccine-related tweets from the Delta rebound window, with an extended analysis across three pandemic windows totaling 182,053 tweets. Sentiment was operationalized using two complementary models: VADER (lexicon-based) and Twitter-RoBERTa. Latent topics were extracted using BERTopic. Engagement was modeled with a Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial (ZINB) specification with eleven predictors. Results. Media richness (URL presence) was the strongest content-level predictor of engagement (IRR = 4.56, p < 0.001). All three dialogic markers were negatively associated with engagement: question presence (IRR = 0.76), hashtag count (IRR = 0.87 per tag), mention count (IRR = 0.89 per mention). This dialogic paradox held across all three pandemic windows and mirrors Zhang et al.'s Weibo findings, indicating cross-platform convergence. Positive sentiment had a modest effect that approximately doubled between tools (VADER IRR = 1.37 vs RoBERTa IRR = 1.91). The extended analysis revealed a phase-dependent reversal in the media-richness effect: beta = +1.26 at Delta peak but beta = -0.37 in the post-Delta inter-peak window (Wald z = 61.9, p < 0.001). Conclusions. During peak-uncertainty crisis phases, informational richness outperforms dialogic engagement — a pattern that contradicts DCT's direct predictions but replicates across platforms. Media Richness Theory requires reformulation with a crisis-phase parameter. For public health communicators, prioritizing URL-bearing content over conversational engagement markers is the strongest single lever identified in this study.

title: Contact with Extraterrestrial Intelligence – Results from a Global Survey about Projected Perceptions and Reactions among the World’s Societies
authors: Michael Bohlander, Anton, Andreas, John Elliott
abstract: In 2024, the authors carried out a survey to canvass global views about what the future for humans would look like once contact with extraterrestrial intelligence had been made. The aim of the survey was thus not merely the typical set of questions often found in other surveys, i.e., whether people believe in the existence of aliens, what or who they are, or where they come from etc., although it contained a set of such questions. These were included for the purpose of situating the answers to the essential questions within the context of different parts of societies, capturing their expectations of how diverse kinds of contact events would affect them personally, and how they thought the relationship with an alien species could develop, especially with regard to certain ethical issues.

title: The Shadow of Saddam: The 1968 Coup and the Bonapartism of the Baath Party
abstract: This paper explores the extent to which Bonapartist dynamics influenced the Baath Party’s state-building project in Iraq following the 1968 coup. Focusing on the rule of Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr, it investigates the contradiction between the Baath Party’s ideological commitment to Arab unity, socialism, and popular democracy, and its increasing reliance on military power and authoritarian control. Using a qualitative, historically grounded analysis of speeches, party reports, and state documents, and drawing from Marxist theory, particularly the concept of Bonapartism, the study argues that al-Bakr’s regime exhibited key Bonapartist traits: the centralisation of authority, fusion of military and political leadership, and the use of populist-revolutionary rhetoric to mask coercive governance. Some deviations were observed, such as the absence of overt foreign adventurism and a continued, if constrained, role for party institutions. Power, however, became more kinship-related than military, with the Tikriti clan dominating the state. The groundwork laid during al-Bakr’s rule, by placing Tikriti kinsmen in high positions, directly enabled Saddam Hussein’s eventual authoritarian dominance. While certain ideological elements persisted in rhetoric and social policy, they were subordinated to regime consolidation. The findings suggest that Bonapartism is best viewed not as a rigid model but as a heuristic for exploring how revolutionary legitimacy can be co-opted to justify coercive state-building in periods of instability.

title: Did Brexit Travel? Eurosceptic Parties across Europe on Facebook after the 2016 Referendum
abstract: Eurosceptic parties across Europe might be expected to have drawn attention from the United Kingdom's vote to leave the European Union on 23 June 2016. I test whether engagement with the Facebook pages of Eurosceptic parties and leaders in 19 other European countries changed around the referendum and later Brexit milestones, using CrowdTangle data. I compare 37 Eurosceptic pages, classified with the PopuList, with other pages in the same country and week in a 25-week window around the vote (42,265 posts from 143 pages). Posts mentioning Brexit or the UK rose from under 1% to about 9% of posts in the two weeks after the vote, but equally for Eurosceptic and other pages. Engagement per post did not change differentially in those two weeks (−0.02 log points, SE 0.11), nor did the mix of reactions. Eurosceptic pages posted about 16% less than other pages in those weeks, but similar dips appear in late June 2014, 2017 and 2018. Of five later milestones, only the March 2019 extension gave a clearly positive estimate, about 23%, but it does not survive clustering by country or adjustment for testing both outcomes, coincides with the European Parliament campaign, and came without more posts about Brexit. In the United Kingdom itself, interactions per post with all parties' pages roughly doubled relative to pages elsewhere. On Facebook, Brexit was a large British event and a shared topic abroad, but I find no sign that it lifted Eurosceptic parties elsewhere relative to their rivals. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

title: Knowing or Believing? Political Interest, Institutional Trust and Turnout in the Arab World
abstract: Does trust in national institutions make people more likely to vote, or does attention to politics matter more? The literature points both ways for the Arab world, where elections take place in contexts of contested legitimacy. Using Wave VII of the Arab Barometer (2021-2022), this paper tests the association between self-reported turnout, trust in the national government and political interest among 19,525 respondents in the nine countries with valid data on all items. In logistic regressions with country fixed effects, a one-point increase in political interest (four-point scale) is associated with a 7.1 percentage-point higher probability of reporting having voted, against 2.3 points for trust. The interest effect is positive in every country but varies significantly in size, from above 10 points in Morocco and Lebanon to near zero in Jordan and Sudan. A cluster analysis of trust in four institutions shows that only broad, consistent trust goes with higher turnout; selective trust looks much like distrust. Results hold across 128 alternative specifications. All estimates are associational.
